name: Curse of Unyielding Mist
summary: Solar Circle (Circle of Adamant) spell. The sorcerer who invokes this vile malediction inflicts upon an area a fog that will not lift. The mist blocks out most light and casts the region into a perpetual twilight, a gloom of unparalleled strength.
requirements: Solar Circle Sorcery -- no confirmed Abyssal-accessible enabling Charm exists in either source book; catalogued for reference only (see this row's notes).
mechanics: The sorcerer who invokes this vile malediction inflicts upon an area a fog that will not lift. The mist blocks out most light and casts the region into a perpetual twilight, a gloom of unparalleled strength. From the outside, the unyielding mist appears to be a single thick gray cloud 100 feet high, similar to a normal mist but more substantial. Inside, it is quite different from normal fog. Light is dimmed during the day, but the fog is slightly luminescent at night, and a diffused light fills the air at all times. Night and day merge into one dour pall, making it difficult to tell time. The mist also has an unusual, acrid scent to it that is reminiscent of brimstone. To cast the curse, a sorcerer must stand at the border of the region toward which she wishes ill and name that area in a spell that takes only a minute to recite. While she speaks, her Essence forms a hazy silver outline about her, through which tiny sparks of purple lightning trace. As she continues the conjuration, small tendrils of fog form within this aura and begin to snake out along the ground toward the targeted region. The targeted region can be no larger than 10 square miles per point of permanent Essence the caster possesses, and the area must all fall under a single name by which the common people know it. When she completes the spell, the sorcerer names a condition by which the curse may be lifted, such as a marriage, pregnancy, admittance of guilt to a crime or action or some other suitably dramatic event. While the mist holds sway over a territory, several effects occur: • Visibility is severely hampered. Clear vision ends at about a yard in the mist, and murky vision at about five yards. Beyond five yards, it is nearly impossible to make anything out. Murky vision increases any attack difficulties by 1. Beyond the murky vision range, attacks are made as if blind, with a +2 increase in difficulty. These difficulties are environmental. In addition, tracking foes through the mist becomes nearly impossible, adding 3 to the difficulty of any mundane attempt to track a creature. Due to its sorcerous and confusing nature, supernatural trackers suffer a +1 difficulty to any rolls made for them to track an opponent through the unyielding mist. • Moods are altered. The perpetual pall of fog, day in and day out, begins to depress and dishearten all of those within it. Soon after the mist takes hold, social interactions with and between residents of the afflicted region become strained. Dice pool rolls involving social interactions all suffer a two-die penalty. Make a Valor check each day for Exalts and other Essence wielders within the mist for them to ignore this penalty. • Plant growth is inhibited. Without sunlight, the flora of the cursed area slowly withers and dies. Crops are ruined, and even ancient forests cannot withstand the power of the mist for more than a few years. • Fungus proliferates. As indigenous plants die, many bizarre species of fungi spread rapidly. After only a few days beneath the mist, mildew can be found growing on untended surfaces. After a week, a blacking film similar to rust covers the faç ades of buildings. Tree bark produces earshaped shelf mushrooms, while dark places become home to nameless slimes. After a month, these foul growths begin to erode the surfaces on which they fester. Even if the fungus is removed, stonework and metalwork appears discolored and pitted. After six months, the fungi reach inside houses and domiciles, spreading overnight to the floors and walls of any except the most frequented of chambers. After a year, sleeping people have to clean germinated spores off of themselves when they wake in the morning. All fungi that grow in the mists taste foul and are inedible. Slaying the caster of the curse is not enough to forcibly end its reign — it is susceptible only to the intervention of the Incarna and to Adamant Countermagic cast during the initial casting. Otherwise, the unyielding mist remains for eternity — or until the caster's condition is met.
compatibility: Target: One city, town or region.

name: Essence Inversion
summary: Solar Circle (Circle of Adamant) spell. All things in Creation were formed out of the vast chaos of Essence that came before time, shaped by the dreams and the will of the Primordials and governed by the Celestial Hierarchy. A savant who has studied Creation closely understands the interactions of the Essence that make up all things — and how Essence fuels life.
requirements: Solar Circle Sorcery -- no confirmed Abyssal-accessible enabling Charm exists in either source book; catalogued for reference only (see this row's notes).
mechanics: All things in Creation were formed out of the vast chaos of Essence that came before time, shaped by the dreams and the will of the Primordials and governed by the Celestial Hierarchy. A savant who has studied Creation closely understands the interactions of the Essence that make up all things — and how Essence fuels life. That understanding led to the creation of this spell, which starts a chain reaction in the target's own Essence that, if left unchecked, will annihilate it utterly. The sorcerer's player must make an Intelligence + Occult roll for the Exalt when the spell is cast, in case the victim wishes to parry or dodge the attack. Creatures targeted by Essence Inversion can only parry or dodge this spell with Charms, and no mortal creature can escape the sorcerer's wrath. The caster gathers her Essence into a twisting beam of dark purple and black, which shoots forth from her hands to strike the spell's target. When it hits, it explodes into bands of the same dark purple and black that wrap around the victim's torso and constrict, fading as they merge with the target's own Essence. On the turn after the spell is cast and the beam strikes, the target feels its Essence begin to churn and rebel within him. If he is an Exalt, his anima banner will flare, but instead of the usual color, it will be flecked with purple and black blotches, like bruises. The victim then suffers 10L damage every turn after the spell is cast, until he dies, until the spell is countered or until the caster dispels the inversion. This damage can be soaked only with Stamina and Charms. As the spell's effects progress and the victim takes more damage, its aura or anima banner will turn completely to the dark purple and black colors with which the sorcerer struck the target. When the victim finally dies from the Essence Inversion, its body implodes, leaving no physical remains.

Any creature standing directly next to or being carried by the target is shaken free when the cylinder of earth breaks free of the ground and begins to rise, so that it will not be damaged by the spell's effects.

name: Incantation of the Invincible Army
summary: Solar Circle (Circle of Adamant) spell. Through the use of this spell, the sorcerer invokes the blessing of the Unconquered Sun and the Five Maidens for her allies and removes such favor from her enemies. By channeling the light of the sun and stars toward friendly forces, the caster both increases the skill and might of allies and decimates the power and morale of their opponents.
requirements: Solar Circle Sorcery -- no confirmed Abyssal-accessible enabling Charm exists in either source book; catalogued for reference only (see this row's notes).
mechanics: Through the use of this spell, the sorcerer invokes the blessing of the Unconquered Sun and the Five Maidens for her allies and removes such favor from her enemies. By channeling the light of the sun and stars toward friendly forces, the caster both increases the skill and might of allies and decimates the power and morale of their opponents. Allies of the sorcerer targeted by this spell gain one dot to all Physical Attributes for the duration of the spell, while any being opposing a target of the incantation suffers a one-die penalty to attacks, dodges, parries and Valor checks while engaged in combat. If using the Mail and Steel rules, increase by 1 the Valor, Drill, Attack Traits and Might of all stacks allied with the caster. The caster chants with her arms raised for the three turns it takes to cast the spell, and her anima banner flares toward the heavens. A golden aura rises to the sky to clear any clouds and rain from the battlefield and to allow the light of the sun and stars to shine down over the battle. When the incantation is complete, the flow of light is reversed, and the light from the heavens pours down on the sorcerer. Then, it strikes out in narrow beams that illuminate each of the targets of the spell. The caster may invoke the blessing for up to 5,000 creatures per point of permanent Essence she possesses. She must keep her hands raised for the duration of the spell and can take no other actions for the scene except concentrate on the blessing and the battle at hand. For each hour the battle persists, the caster's player must make a reflexive Stamina + Endurance roll, with a difficulty equal to the number of hours the battle has lasted, for the sorcerer to remain in position. If the sorcerer suffers an attack, her player must make a successful Stamina + Resistance roll, with a difficulty equal to the number of health levels of damage she takes, for the Exalt to keep her concentration, or she loses control of the spell. If a roll to maintain concentration fails, then, for the remainder of the turn, the blessing is lost, but she may regain control of it by her player making another Stamina + Endurance or Stamina + Resistance roll, with the same difficulty +1. If successful, the sorcerer is able to regain control of the spell, but if she fails again, or if any roll botches, then the spell is ended, and the blessing is lost. The effects of the invocation end if the sorcerer loses concentration or is slain, if the spell is countered, if the caster dispels the effect or at the end of the battle in which the targets are participating. At the end of the spell's effects, the caster's player must make a successful reflexive Stamina roll with a difficulty equal to the number of hours that the sorcerer remained in concentration, or she passes out from fatigue. If this Stamina roll fails, then the sorcerer must sleep for a number of days equal to the amount by which the Stamina roll was failed.

name: Total Annihilation
summary: Solar Circle (Circle of Adamant) spell. No single spell demonstrates the sheer power and destructive force of the Solars like this one does. The sorcerer holds out her hand, and an emerald mist of Essence swirls about her, gathering into an opalescent green orb about the size of an apple in her palm.
requirements: Solar Circle Sorcery -- no confirmed Abyssal-accessible enabling Charm exists in either source book; catalogued for reference only (see this row's notes).
mechanics: No single spell demonstrates the sheer power and destructive force of the Solars like this one does. The sorcerer holds out her hand, and an emerald mist of Essence swirls about her, gathering into an opalescent green orb about the size of an apple in her palm. The caster then hurls the orb up to 200 yards away, her player making a Dexterity + Occult or a Dexterity + Thrown roll for the sorcerer to hit her target. Where the emerald sphere strikes, it explodes into a column of bright green light 50 yards wide and five miles high, which deals 50 lethal health levels of damage to everything it touches. The destructive energy then expands on the same initiative count as the explosion occurred at a rate of 50 yards in diameter each turn for a number of turns equal to the caster's permanent Essence. Everything caught in the expanding emerald field of destruction takes 25 lethal health levels of damage for every turn it is bathed in the emerald energy. Creatures near the explosion may abort their actions to try to outrun the lethal energy. The orb created in the casting of Total Annihilation can only be parried or dodged through the use of Charms. Any mortal weapon that attempts to parry the sphere will trigger its explosion. If the orb is successfully parried with a Charm and an enchanted weapon, then it is deflected away from the target and will land in a random direction 1,000 yards away. Once the orb explodes, the effect cannot be parried even with the use of Charms and can only be dodged by a perfect defense such as Seven Shadows Evasion or soaked with a Charm such as Adamant Skin Technique. Though this spell's damaging effects last for more than one turn, such perfect-defense Charms will protect an Exalt from all damage. Total Annihilation may be countered successfully only while it is being cast. Once the orb of Essence is created, then casting Adamant Countermagic against it will only reflect the spell as if it were parried with a magical weapon, not interrupt it.

name: Wrath of the Five Elements
summary: Solar Circle (Circle of Adamant) spell. This spell calls upon the power of the Five Elemental Dragons to smite the caster's enemy with five sorcerous attacks. When the spell is cast, the sorcerer's player makes a single Intelligence + Occult roll, marking the number of successes, which becomes the difficulty to resist the spell's effects.
requirements: Solar Circle Sorcery -- no confirmed Abyssal-accessible enabling Charm exists in either source book; catalogued for reference only (see this row's notes).
mechanics: This spell calls upon the power of the Five Elemental Dragons to smite the caster's enemy with five sorcerous attacks. When the spell is cast, the sorcerer's player makes a single Intelligence + Occult roll, marking the number of successes, which becomes the difficulty to resist the spell's effects. If the caster fails to garner any successes, then his prayers have been unanswered, and the Essence cost of the spell is expended with no effect. If the sorcerer is successful, then the spell's elemental attacks will follow the target wherever she goes and strike the victim on the sorcerer's initiative. The sorcerer chants a prayer to the Five Elemental Dragons and points at the being he wishes to target. The air around that creature heats and sparks for a moment before a tongue of livid red flame lashes the victim. This magical fire deals 15L damage to the target and also incinerates her belongings. Any unenchanted flammable material that the creature bears is destroyed, including the straps and bindings on non-magical armor. This fire reduces the target's armor soak by 3. At the beginning of the next turn, after the flames subside, the air turns chilly, and a blue mist rises, just before a solid chunk of ice forms about the body of the victim. This cold deals 15L damage that may only be soaked with the target's Stamina and any effects that add to natural soak. If even one health level of damage is successfully inflicted, then the target has its movement rate and jumping distance halved until the end of the scene. At the beginning of the turn after the ice forms, it melts into the ground and thorn-covered vines sprout to wrap about the target, prying beneath any remaining clothing and armor. The thorns on the vines deal 5L damage that can only be soaked by the creature's Stamina (plus any appropriate Charms) but are envenomed. The victim's player must make a successful reflexive Stamina + Resistance roll, or her character is stricken by this venom, which deals no damage, but causes the target to suffer a four-die penalty to all actions until the end of the scene. The difficulty of this roll is equal to the sorcerer's player's successes on the Intelligence + Occult roll. The vines quickly dry and crumble at the beginning of the next turn. Then, the earth quakes, and three giant pillars of stone, each eight feet tall, rise from the earth and slam together against the victim, dealing a total of 20 health levels of bashing damage. The victim's player must make a successful Dexterity + Athletics roll to avoid having her character knocked down by the pillars, with a difficulty equal to the caster's successes on the Intelligence + Occult roll. (See Exalted, pp. 234-235, for more information on knockdown and fighting while prone.) On the final turn of the spell's effects, the pillars slide back into the earth, and a geyser of water erupts beneath the target. The rushing water batters and chokes the victim, causing five lethal health levels of damage, which ignores armor. In addition, when the water fades and evaporates at the end of the turn, the victim is left unable to speak or to invoke Charms for a number of turns equal to the caster's permanent Essence. Each of the elemental attacks of this spell may be dodged or parried only with the use of Charms, and since each attack is separate, the target's player must make the appropriate roll for each spell effect.

summary: Sample Hearthstone (Level 3, Type: Sidereal). Despite its dull, gray and uninspiring appearance, this Hearthstone will allow an Exalt to stay awake as long as she wishes, without feeling tired or suffering any deterioration is her physical or mental abilities.

A botch gives the character a temporary derangement, which endures until she goes without using the Ever-Open Eye for the same length of times as she was using it continually before the botch.

name: Hearthstone Formation, Theme and Expression Rules
summary: Chapter Three's Manse/Hearthroom framework: how Hearthstones form in a Manse's Hearthroom (or, more slowly and at reduced level, in a raw Demesne), how a Manse's Essence flow links to its Hearthstone(s), and the Theme/Expression system architects use to shape a Hearthstone's powers.
requirements: Manse or Demesne Background framework; not itself a selectable power. Supports the Hearthstone catalog rows above.
mechanics: Each Manse focuses Essence into physical form at its Hearthroom, the geomantic center of the building, where Essence flow is so intense it crystallizes into a Hearthstone -- a gem roughly the size of a hen's egg, heavier than its size suggests, beautifully cut, and often glowing with inner fire. Hearthstones take two weeks per level to form, and only while a disk of one of the Five Magical Materials sits at the formation point; removing, destroying or damaging that disk halts formation, and interrupting formation by removing the gem early yields a Hearthstone whose level equals the number of complete weeks of formation passed. A Manse can instead be designed to produce multiple Hearthstones simultaneously (the sum of their levels can never exceed the Manse's level), a method often used by Dragon-Blooded Dynasts gifting a single Manse to several children; a Manse will not produce further Hearthstones beyond that sum until one or more of the existing ones are destroyed, at which point a replacement immediately begins forming (unless the Manse has fallen into disrepair). Hearthstones can also form, by accident or design, in a raw Demesne if its Essence flows focus on a small area containing a quantity of one of the Five Magical Materials; such a Demesne Hearthstone takes two months per level of the Demesne to form, is always one level less than the Demesne, and decays into uselessness within a number of weeks equal to the Demesne's level once removed from it. A permanent Essence link binds a Manse to its Hearthstone(s) at all times, letting Essence flow from the Manse to whoever holds the stone; this link also lets an attuned Exalt trace a Hearthstone back to its source Manse, and a Hearthstone Compass (see Aspect Book: Earth) lets even an unattuned Exalt do the same. Each Hearthstone's powers beyond simple Essence-channeling are defined by a Theme (a single-word concept the architect bakes into the Manse's Essence via artwork and design, such as health, travel, luck, shelter, relationships, fear, leadership or light) and an Expression (the concrete mechanical effect that Theme takes, such as a fear-themed stone that scares off nearby animals or grants extra dice to resist intimidation). Multiple Hearthstones from the same Manse always share a Theme but have different Expressions; Expressions can be changed per the rules on Exalted p. 247. Redesigning a Manse to change a Hearthstone's Theme entirely is extremely difficult, requiring an Intelligence + Occult roll at difficulty (3 + the Manse's level).
compatibility: Framework/system text, not a target-bearing effect.
notes: Chapter Three: Demesne and Manse, 'Hearthstones'/'Hearthrooms'/'The Manse-Hearthstone Link'/'Hearthstone Properties' sections, pp. 66-68 (PDF 67-69), Savant and Sorcerer. Catalogued as a single reference-only framework row (matching this project's precedent for necromancy-framework-and-circles) rather than transcribed rule-by-rule, since it is system context supporting the 15 Sample Hearthstone rows above rather than itself a selectable power.

name: Artifact Creation Framework (Materials, Exotic Ingredients, Attunement Extrapolation)
summary: Chapter Two's artifact-creation rules: crafting with each of the Five Magical Materials (including the setting lore on how starmetal and orichalcum are obtained/refined in the Second Age), the requirement that every artifact use one or more 'exotic ingredients' as a sympathetic seed for its effect (with sample First Age and Age of Sorrows ingredient lists), and the Intelligence + Occult/Lore rolls required to back-extrapolate lost First Age ingredient techniques.
requirements: GM/crafting-system framework; not itself a selectable power. Supports the Sample Artifacts catalog rows below and any future custom-artifact creation the Storyteller adjudicates.
mechanics: Every artifact's core must be one or more of the Five Magical Materials (jade, moonsilver, orichalcum, starmetal, soulsteel), each gated behind its own crafting tradition -- e.g. orichalcum is refined from natural gold in a lava-heated solar forge with sunlight focused via occult mirrors (Intelligence + Craft (Orichalcum), difficulty 3), while starmetal is refined from the executed Essence of small gods condemned by the Bureau of Destiny's audits and can otherwise be worked with mundane tools. Beyond the Magical Material core, the Laws of Creation require every artifact to incorporate additional 'exotic ingredients' that inform its purpose and focus its Essence -- symbolically or sympathetically appropriate objects (not necessarily physical: tapping a Demesne or rechanneling a dragon track both qualify) that hint at the artifact's function; the book lists five sample First Age exotic ingredients (distorted-demon blood for delving beyond Creation and piercing demons' defenses; elemental salt-diamonds that remove an artifact's Drawback when consumed in its forging; a perfect sword-kata etched onto glass and traced onto weapons, adding two dice to Melee attack pools; Demesne-embodying rods that let an artifact function like a portable Manse; Sidereal prayer-threads; Solar-corpse bones for necromantic feedback loops; dragon's blood; Heaven's quintessence/ambrosia; bottled Wyld; and lightning-fused obsidian) and ten sample Age of Sorrows substitutes (ground dust of broken artifacts reducing construction difficulty by 2; vented failed-Hearthstone energy reducing an Essence Drawback by two dots; Fair Folk-blood flowers that infuse the maker's Virtues if 4+; and others). Because Solars mostly used synthetic, purpose-built Essence seeds rather than natural ingredients, a modern artificer working from surviving First Age designs must succeed at an Intelligence + Occult roll (difficulty 3 for Artifact Level one through three, difficulty 4 for Level four and five) to correctly back-extrapolate what natural ingredient can substitute for a seed the Second Age can no longer synthesize.
compatibility: Framework/system text, not a target-bearing effect.
notes: Chapter Two: Artifice and Enchantment, pp. 21-41 (PDF 22-42), Savant and Sorcerer. Summarized at framework granularity (matching this project's precedent for necromancy-framework-and-circles and hearthstone-formation-and-theme-rules) rather than transcribed section-by-section, since it is GM-facing crafting-system context rather than a directly selectable power; the chapter's setting-lore passages on each Magical Material's Second Age sourcing (starmetal's grim origin in particular) and its two exotic-ingredient sample lists are the most distinctive player-relevant flavor and are summarized above. A single generic Merit found in this chapter, 'Moonsilver Initiate' (5-pt Merit, 2-pt for Lunars, p. 20/PDF 21, granting knowledge of moonsilver-crafting secrets), is not Abyssal-specific and is out of this splat's core scope, consistent with this inventory's existing confirmed-absent finding for Abyssal-specific Merits/Flaws in the core book; it is noted here rather than given its own row.

name: Collar of Dawn's Cleansing Light
summary: Sample Artifact (Artifact •). This artifact comes in a variety of forms -- studded bands, chokers, collars, torcs, delicate necklaces and the like -- any piece of neck jewelry is appropriate, and these items are still quite common today.
requirements: Artifact Background (see the artifact's rating for cost).
mechanics: This artifact comes in a variety of forms -- studded bands, chokers, collars, torcs, delicate necklaces and the like -- any piece of neck jewelry is appropriate, and these items are still quite common today. Many of the Dragon-Blooded in the Second Age own and wear them where possible, not just for their useful properties but also to show off. Being able to casually wear an artifact, even a weak one, is a powerful statement. The purpose of the collar is to keep the wearer clean inside and out. She could spend weeks living beneath a rubbish heap and emerge at the end as if she had just spent hours preparing for a grand ball. The artifact negates all penalties to Social rolls that would be applied due to the character being dirty or unkempt. Attuning to the collar extends its powers beyond the Exalt's clothing to her physical body. The artifact's cleansing light adds two dice to Resistance rolls against disease or poison (see Exalted, p. 243). All of the Five Magical Materials have been used to construct these wonders, even soulsteel, so any kind of Exalt should be able to find one to suit her tastes. The collar requires the commitment of 1 mote of Essence to become active.

name: Ring of Being
summary: Sample Artifact (Artifact ••••). The great Twilight artificer Jervon made a number of these rings during the height of the First Age.
requirements: Artifact Background (see the artifact's rating for cost).
mechanics: The great Twilight artificer Jervon made a number of these rings during the height of the First Age. He worked for years at his great forge deep within the Imperial Mountain, focusing the power of the center of Creation into these beautiful artifacts. The history of some of them is well known. For instance, the single orichalcum ring known to have existed was always worn by the Hierophant of the Solar Deliberative. It is rumored that other examples of this powerful artifact made of different Magical Materials were given as presents or rewards to certain Lunar, Sidereal and Terrestrial Exalted. There are no known soulsteel rings of being as the secret of their creation was lost long before the Deathlords rose to eminence. It is said that each ring was a pure and perfect representation of the Magical Material from which it was made. A moonsilver ring would shine like a star under the light of Luna, and looking into a ring of black jade would be like looking into the deepest ocean. The rings were never sullied with adornments or jewels, their beauty and power were enough on their own. The power of these rings is great but highly focused. No magic or power of the dead, the Fair Folk, demons, spirits or the Wyld can affect the wearer's innate form or mind. She can be hurt by physical attacks or effects, but neither the native Charms of a spirit nor the chaotic nature of the Wyld could change her, no spell might addle her mind or make her love someone, and no demon may ever claim her soul while she is attuned to the artifact. The act of attunement is costly. Fifteen motes must be invested, but that is a small price to pay. In addition, an Exalt can only attune to a ring made of the appropriate Magical Material. While the amount of the relevant Magical Material needed to forge the ring is relatively small, the added ingredients are difficult to come by at best -- at least one sample of the Deep Wyld is needed and possibly also a fragment of the Labyrinth that exists in the dark Underworld.

Explicitly noted as having no known soulsteel examples ("the secret of their creation was lost long before the Deathlords rose to eminence"), so an Abyssal PC could not normally acquire a soulsteel Ring of Being through ordinary means -- flagged here rather than excluded outright, since a Storyteller could still rule that an Abyssal wears one forged of a different Magical Material, or that a Deathlord has rediscovered the soulsteel variant as a plot device.

name: Wings of the Raptor
summary: Sample Artifact (Artifact ••••). When an earthbound Solar wished to join his Lunar love high above the earth, he set to building the first set of these wings.
requirements: Artifact Background (see the artifact's rating for cost).
mechanics: When an earthbound Solar wished to join his Lunar love high above the earth, he set to building the first set of these wings. At times when they are not being used, the wings appear as a heavy cloak, but with the expenditure of 10 motes of Essence, the cloak grants its wearer the power of flight. A transformation takes place, changing the garment into a glorious set of wings 20 feet across from wingtip to wingtip. This spent Essence cannot be reclaimed until the wings are returned to their mundane state. When flying with these wings, an Exalt may move at five times his base running speed (80 miles per hour flying) and adds six dice to any Dexterity roll involving aerial maneuvering, including dodging and hand-to-hand combat. In addition, he gains six extra dice on all sight-based Perception rolls, and all modifiers due to distance are reduced by three. Characters using the wings can only be attacked in hand-to-hand combat during the initiative tick when they attack a foe in hand-to-hand combat. If flying characters choose to linger outside of hand-to-hand range and characters cannot leap to them or otherwise come to grips, the airborne characters have control of the situation. A target may attack (or counterattack) without penalty. Characters other than the target who wish to attack must be able to move into hand-to-hand range reflexively and suffer a -3 penalty. Characters who have long weapons such as spears suffer only a -1 penalty. A flying character may be attacked in ranged combat normally.

name: Soul Mirror
summary: Sample Artifact (Artifact •••••). Soul Mirror is, without a doubt, one of the most horrifying weapons in Creation.
requirements: Artifact Background (see the artifact's rating for cost).
mechanics: Soul Mirror is, without a doubt, one of the most horrifying weapons in Creation. It was forged centuries ago by the Lover Clad in Raiment of Tears to be carried by her champion, but her nemissary fell to two incomparable Dragon-Blooded martial artists, and the sword was lost. The weapon appears, at first glance, to be a mere soulsteel grand daiklave. Although the blade is flat and black, no souls may be seen in its surface, nor can the voices of those used in its forging be heard. The same amount of Essence is required to attune to Soul Mirror as to a grand daiklave, and all of Soul Mirror's statistics are the same as the blade whose shape it shares (see Exalted, p. 342). The only noticeable difference is the additional Hearthstone setting on the handle (for a total of four). If it strikes an opponent, Soul Mirror will drain one point of temporary Willpower and a number of motes of Essence equal to its wielder's permanent Essence. Half of the motes (round down) are passed to the bearer of the blade, while the rest are consumed by the sword. The true horror of this unholy artifact is only seen when it takes a life. Instead of the ghost of the victim going to the Underworld or submitting to Lethe, it is drawn into Soul Mirror. Until this soul is consumed, it will be visible in the flat blade of the daiklave, tormented and afraid. However, at any time, the wielder may allow the sword to consume the soul, thus adding 1 to the weapon's speed, accuracy and damage for seven days. Only four consumed souls may provide such a benefit at any given time. The player of anyone who faces Soul Mirror in battle must succeed at a Willpower roll, or he suffers a four-die penalty to any attack rolls. The roll is difficulty 4 for mortals, 3 for Exalted and other magical beings and 2 for Solars or Abyssals. The final power of the daiklave is perhaps what makes it so valuable and so dangerous. As a reflexive action at the cost of one of the souls contained within the sword and all of the bearer's remaining peripheral Essence, any single attack that would damage the wielder to Incapacitated or below may be ignored. This action will cause anima flare and can only be invoked if at least 10 Essence remain in the Exalt's Peripheral Essence pool. As this action is performed and the soul within the blade emits its final scream of agony, all damage from the fatal strike is ignored, any lethal or bashing damage the bearer of the blade has suffered is healed, and she will also heal a number of aggravated levels of damage equal to her permanent Essence.

Directly relevant to this splat: it is a soulsteel grand daiklave, explicitly calls out Abyssals (alongside Solars) as facing the lowest difficulty-2 fear roll when wielded against them, and its soul-devouring nature and Deathlord provenance (forged by the Lover Clad in Raiment of Tears) make it a natural fit for an Abyssal PC or antagonist artifact.

name: Warstriders: Overview, Benefits, Limitations and Piloting Rules
summary: The Appendix's general warstrider framework: what a warstrider is (a giant, Essence-driven suit of armor, not a vehicle), its mechanical benefits (Strength, Endurance, Heavy Armor, Durability) and limitations (Size, Massive Weapons, Mobility, Limited Manipulation/Vision, Essence costs, Maintenance), who can pilot one and how (including an explicit rule for the dead/ghosts), and its interaction with Hearthstones and Charms.
requirements: Framework/system overview supporting the warstrider-class-* and proteus-gauntlet rows below; not itself a directly selectable item (a specific class of warstrider is the actual acquirable Artifact).
mechanics: Warstriders are giant humanoid suits of Essence-driven armor -- not vehicles -- typically 16 to 25 feet tall, built by the First Age's factory-cathedrals and still slowly produced today at a trickle. They are powered by Essence-driven enchantments rather than the wearer's muscles: even the weakest warstrider is roughly twice as strong as the mightiest mortal, and any Charm that enhances the wearer's Strength also applies to the warstrider. Wearing one is not fatiguing (the armor can lock its limbs to let the pilot rest), and its heavy armor grants substantial soak that, unlike normal armor, means an attack that fails to exceed that soak deals the wearer no damage at all; warstriders are also unusually durable, never treated as inanimate objects for damage purposes. Warstriders multiply the wearer's movement rate by 10 and are treated as armor (not vehicles) for purposes of Charms that ward possessions against the Wyld. Limitations balance these benefits: a warstrider's bulk makes its wearer 'half-blind' with only a vague sense of her own limbs, its size imposes a three-success penalty on attacks against targets under 10 feet tall, incidental collisions can inadvertently smash the surroundings, its massive built-in weapons are easily dodged by anything smaller than itself, and a warstrider's Strength may only be used for combat damage, lifting/carrying, breaking objects and jumping distance (the wearer's own Strength applies to everything else). Any being able to channel and commit Essence to artifacts can attune to and pilot a warstrider, but several categories face special rules: a materializing spirit whose panoply includes a warstrider may manifest already wearing and attuned to it; the dead may only control warstriders while materialized in the land of the living or while inhabiting a corpse's body, and they pay double the normal Essence commitment to attune to a warstrider not made of soulsteel; hungry ghosts normally lack the discipline to pilot one at all; the Fair Folk make no use of warstriders by choice, though an individual fae could attune to one; and mortals/God-Blooded with the appropriate Merits can attune to warstriders under the normal rules, though their lack of Charms and limited Essence constrain their usefulness. Warstriders can also shift to a Low-Power Stance to reduce maintenance and Hearthstone requirements at the cost of combat effectiveness, and they require an hour of maintenance per 10 hours of operation (with combat/heavy-labor hours counting double), performed by a technician with Lore •••••, Occult •••• and Craft (First Age Weapons) •••• and Resources •••• worth of tools; falling behind on maintenance imposes escalating mechanical penalties (reduced soak, speed, and a growing die penalty) until repaired.
compatibility: Framework/system text, not a target-bearing effect.
notes: Appendix: Warstriders, pp. 145-153 (PDF 146-154), Savant and Sorcerer. Summarized at framework granularity (matching this project's precedent for necromancy-framework-and-circles), since this content is system/rules context rather than a single selectable item. The 'the dead may only control warstriders...' rule (p. 152/PDF 153) is directly relevant to Abyssal deathknights and their ghost/undead allies and is preserved verbatim above rather than paraphrased away. This project's Chapter Four 'The Deathlords' section (p. 147/PDF 148) also confirms setting-level Abyssal warstrider use: the First and Forsaken Lion fields warstriders extensively in his Legion Sanguinary, the Mask of Winters equips sizable numbers (most worn by war ghosts), and Deathlord-built warstriders 'nearly always have noble or royal warstriders constructed in their name, using secret techniques thought lost since the Usurpation' -- summarized in the warstrider-class-royal and warstrider-class-juggernaut rows below, which carry the most explicit Abyssal-specific flavor text.

name: Warstrider (Scout Class)
summary: Warstrider class. Scout warstriders would seem to be something of a misnomer -- after all, scouts are supposed to be stealthy and quiet, and a 16-foot-tall automaton of steel and jade would hardly seem either.
requirements: Artifact Background (warstriders are large Artifact-rated equipment; exact dot rating is Storyteller-set per this book's silence on a fixed Artifact rating for each class -- see notes) plus the warstrider piloting/attunement rules in warstrider-framework-and-rules.
mechanics: Scout warstriders would seem to be something of a misnomer -- after all, scouts are supposed to be stealthy and quiet, and a 16-foot-tall automaton of steel and jade would hardly seem either. Scout warstriders were never as popular as common warstriders, but they were built in some numbers for those who valued mobility and speed over armor and raw damage dealing. Scout warstriders were frequently enchanted to make them as unobtrusive and hard to locate as possible -- while rarely successful in completely masking their presence, these spells could reduce their chances of being intercepted or detected.
cost: Artifact (rating set by Storyteller; see notes)
compatibility: See warstrider-framework-and-rules for shared benefits/limitations (Strength, Endurance, Heavy Armor, Mobility x10, Size penalties, Maintenance, etc.).
notes: Appendix: Warstriders, 'Classes of Warstriders', p. 148 (PDF 149), Savant and Sorcerer. This book presents five classes (Scout, Common, Noble, Royal, Juggernaut) as flavor/scale categories with prose descriptions of size, role and rarity rather than restating full mechanical stat blocks or a fixed Artifact-dot rating in this Appendix; marked 'selectable' since a class of warstrider is the acquirable Artifact item a character would take via the Artifact Background, with the Storyteller assigning an appropriate rating (Common being the lowest, Royal/Juggernaut the highest) consistent with the book's own text.

name: Warstrider (Common Class)
summary: Warstrider class. Common warstriders formed the backbone of most Shogunate military units.
requirements: Artifact Background (warstriders are large Artifact-rated equipment; exact dot rating is Storyteller-set per this book's silence on a fixed Artifact rating for each class -- see notes) plus the warstrider piloting/attunement rules in warstrider-framework-and-rules.
mechanics: Common warstriders formed the backbone of most Shogunate military units. Standing six yards tall on average, the majority of common, or infantry, warstriders were made of jade for the use of the Terrestrial Exalted. Due to the comparatively large numbers built, common warstriders form the majority of warstriders in the Second Age. Common warstriders also mark the limit of Creation's ability to build new warstriders -- neither the Realm nor Lookshy have built warstriders of other designs since the period immediately after the Shogunate's fall.
cost: Artifact (rating set by Storyteller; see notes)
compatibility: See warstrider-framework-and-rules for shared benefits/limitations (Strength, Endurance, Heavy Armor, Mobility x10, Size penalties, Maintenance, etc.).

name: Warstrider (Noble Class)
summary: Warstrider class. The Celestial Exalted generally used noble warstriders, and in the Age of Sorrows, they are the only Exalted to retain the secrets of their construction -- and even Lunars and Sidereals rarely build these great suits of armor.
requirements: Artifact Background (warstriders are large Artifact-rated equipment; exact dot rating is Storyteller-set per this book's silence on a fixed Artifact rating for each class -- see notes) plus the warstrider piloting/attunement rules in warstrider-framework-and-rules.
mechanics: The Celestial Exalted generally used noble warstriders, and in the Age of Sorrows, they are the only Exalted to retain the secrets of their construction -- and even Lunars and Sidereals rarely build these great suits of armor. Noble warstriders typically stand slightly taller than common suits -- 20 feet, on average. They are normally stronger and more responsive than common warstriders, as well as more heavily armored. The Scarlet Empress' personal warstrider, Unyielding Fury of Righteousness, is a rare example of a noble warstrider built during the Second Age.
cost: Artifact (rating set by Storyteller; see notes)
compatibility: See warstrider-framework-and-rules for shared benefits/limitations (Strength, Endurance, Heavy Armor, Mobility x10, Size penalties, Maintenance, etc.).

name: Warstrider (Royal Class)
summary: Warstrider class. Always rare, royal warstriders are all but unknown save in legend in the Second Age.
requirements: Artifact Background (warstriders are large Artifact-rated equipment; exact dot rating is Storyteller-set per this book's silence on a fixed Artifact rating for each class -- see notes) plus the warstrider piloting/attunement rules in warstrider-framework-and-rules.
mechanics: Always rare, royal warstriders are all but unknown save in legend in the Second Age. Only the Solars and scant handfuls of other Exalted -- mostly Lunars -- ever wore royal suits. Standing as much as 25 feet tall, these massive suits of armor were formidable in their protection and just as formidable in their strength and speed. Only a tiny handful have survived into the Age of Sorrows, and most are unusable, composed of orichalcum and too heavy for Terrestrials to commit the Essence necessary to attune them. The only royal warstriders that have been forged since the Contagion are grim apparitions of soulsteel and Abyssal iron, terrible weapons in the hands of the Deathlord's servants.
cost: Artifact (rating set by Storyteller; see notes)
compatibility: See warstrider-framework-and-rules for shared benefits/limitations (Strength, Endurance, Heavy Armor, Mobility x10, Size penalties, Maintenance, etc.).
notes: Appendix: Warstriders, 'Classes of Warstriders', p. 149 (PDF 150), Savant and Sorcerer. This book presents five classes (Scout, Common, Noble, Royal, Juggernaut) as flavor/scale categories with prose descriptions of size, role and rarity rather than restating full mechanical stat blocks or a fixed Artifact-dot rating in this Appendix; marked 'selectable' since a class of warstrider is the acquirable Artifact item a character would take via the Artifact Background, with the Storyteller assigning an appropriate rating (Common being the lowest, Royal/Juggernaut the highest) consistent with the book's own text. Directly Abyssal-relevant: the only royal-class warstriders forged since the Contagion are explicitly described as soulsteel-and-Abyssal-iron constructs wielded by Deathlord's servants, making this the flagship warstrider class for an Abyssal PC or Deathlord-aligned NPC force.

name: Warstrider (Juggernaut Class)
summary: Warstrider class. The design for juggernaut warstriders took the warstrider penchant for heavy armor and brute strength to its logical conclusion -- these hulking suits, standing only 20 feet tall on average, but nearly twice as wide as a common warstrider, were ponderously slow when compared to other warstriders, but only the great skyships and a handful of ocean-going craft sported more armor, and almost nothing could hope to wrestle one and win.
requirements: Artifact Background (warstriders are large Artifact-rated equipment; exact dot rating is Storyteller-set per this book's silence on a fixed Artifact rating for each class -- see notes) plus the warstrider piloting/attunement rules in warstrider-framework-and-rules.
mechanics: The design for juggernaut warstriders took the warstrider penchant for heavy armor and brute strength to its logical conclusion -- these hulking suits, standing only 20 feet tall on average, but nearly twice as wide as a common warstrider, were ponderously slow when compared to other warstriders, but only the great skyships and a handful of ocean-going craft sported more armor, and almost nothing could hope to wrestle one and win. Juggernauts were designed and used primarily as siege engines and combat engineering units -- they could withstand the brunt of a fortress' attack on the way in and deal massive damage to even the stoutest of First Age construction. Few juggernauts survived the Contagion, and only scant handfuls now exist in the armories of the Realm and Lookshy. A number of Abyssal deathknights use these massive battle machines, mostly those more interested in raw destructive power than in any kind of subtlety.
cost: Artifact (rating set by Storyteller; see notes)
compatibility: See warstrider-framework-and-rules for shared benefits/limitations (Strength, Endurance, Heavy Armor, Mobility x10, Size penalties, Maintenance, etc.).
notes: Appendix: Warstriders, 'Classes of Warstriders', p. 149 (PDF 150), Savant and Sorcerer. This book presents five classes (Scout, Common, Noble, Royal, Juggernaut) as flavor/scale categories with prose descriptions of size, role and rarity rather than restating full mechanical stat blocks or a fixed Artifact-dot rating in this Appendix; marked 'selectable' since a class of warstrider is the acquirable Artifact item a character would take via the Artifact Background, with the Storyteller assigning an appropriate rating (Common being the lowest, Royal/Juggernaut the highest) consistent with the book's own text. Directly Abyssal-relevant: the text explicitly states that a number of Abyssal deathknights favor juggernaut-class warstriders for their raw destructive power.

name: Proteus Gauntlet
summary: Artifact (Artifact ••••). A warstrider-scale moonsilver smashfist that can reshape itself into any standard warstrider-scale weapon on the fly, solving the problem of a warstrider being unable to carry a full armory into the field.
requirements: Artifact Background (Artifact ••••); must be worn/attuned by a warstrider wearer.
mechanics: One problem warstriders face is that it is far more difficult to carry additional weapons to adjust their armament to deal with differing situations -- as most warstrider weapons are twice as tall as a man, only those readily carried by the warstrider are typically brought along. The proteus gauntlet was developed in the First Age to try and deal with this problem. In its default form, a proteus gauntlet is a moonsilver smashfist scaled for a warstrider. When attuned to by a warstrider wearer, the gauntlet can take the form of any standard warstrider-scale weapon as a non-rolled dice action at the cost of 1 mote per shift. If the gauntlet is shifted into the form of a weapon that requires ammunition, it comes equipped with sufficient ammunition for one turn of use (or one load of ammo, in the case of weapons with a magazine). Once this ammunition is expended, the weapon cannot create more ammunition until the existing ammo is retrieved. Attuning to a proteus gauntlet requires 6 motes, and non-Lunars must pay double the normal cost to gain the Magical Material bonus.
compatibility: Requires a warstrider to wear/wield; scales to warstrider-sized weapon forms only.
notes: Appendix: Warstriders, p. 159 (PDF 160), Savant and Sorcerer. Being moonsilver-based, non-Lunar wearers (including Abyssals) pay double the normal Essence cost to gain its Magical Material bonus, per its own text; noted here rather than treated as a blocker, since the gauntlet still functions for any attuned wearer.

name: Warstrider Weapon Options (Hand-to-Hand, Ranged, Artifact-Grade Tables)
summary: The Appendix's warstrider-scale weapon tables: mundane hand-to-hand options (Punch, Kick, Axe, and similar oversized melee weapons), mundane ranged options (bows and siege-scale ammunition types), and artifact-grade hand-to-hand and ranged weapons (Daiklave, Dire Lance, Fire Lance and others) sized for warstriders, plus named accessories such as the Warstrider Shock Ram.
requirements: Equipment tables supporting a warstrider wearer's loadout; not one single selectable item.
mechanics: Pages 155-159 (PDF 156-160) present full Speed/Accuracy/Damage/Defense/Strength/Dexterity/Martial Arts/Cost stat tables for warstrider-scale weapons: a 'Warstrider Hand-to-Hand Weapons' table (Punch, Kick, and mundane oversized melee weapons such as Axe), a 'Warstrider Ranged Weapons' table (bows and arrow types, including standard, broadhead, frog-crotch, fire and other specialty ammunition), a 'Warstrider Artifact Hand-to-Hand Weapons' table (Daiklave, Dire Lance, Fire Lance and other named artifact-grade melee options), and a 'Warstrider Artifact Ranged Weapons' table, along with weapon-location mounting requirements (arm-mounted vs. shoulder-mounted, etc.) and a named accessory, the Warstrider Shock Ram (a green jade smashfist attachment that, when charged for 2 motes per attack, projects the force of a warstrider's punch up to 20 feet using Brawl or Martial Arts, ignoring the normal size-based penalty for hitting smaller targets at that range). A closing section adapts the hand-to-hand weapon table for the Exalted Power Combat variant rules from the Exalted Players Guide.
cost: N/A (see individual weapons within the tables for their own costs/ratings)
compatibility: Requires a warstrider to wield; see warstrider-framework-and-rules for the general size/mounting rules governing these weapons.
notes: Appendix: Warstriders, pp. 155-160 (PDF 156-161), Savant and Sorcerer. Catalogued as a single reference-only summary row at 'reasonable summary granularity' (per this project's convention for large procedural equipment tables, matching how Book of Bone and Ebony's 69-entry artifact catalog and the Exalted Power Combat weapon table elsewhere in this project were handled) rather than transcribing every named weapon and its full stat line as its own row; the Proteus Gauntlet was distinctive enough (a named, individually-described Artifact-rated item) to warrant its own row above instead.

name: Savant and Sorcerer, Chapter One: Magical Theory -- excluded
summary: Chapter One (printed pp. 9-19, PDF 10-20) is entirely narrative/setting lore about the philosophy and history of sorcery -- the meaning of the three sorcerous initiation rites (Terrestrial/Celestial/Solar), schools of magical thought, and the Heptagram academy on the Isle of Voices. It contains no new Charms, Backgrounds, Merits or other player-facing mechanics.
requirements: N/A -- excluded chapter, no mechanics to gate.
mechanics: The chapter opens with the in-fiction myth of how sorcery was first given to the Exalted (echoing Brigid and Prometheus-style myths) and the thematic meaning of each sorcerous initiation: the Terrestrial initiation is about perception and adaptation, the (unnamed in this excerpt) higher initiations demand greater sacrifice and, from the Celestial initiation onward, sacrifices of an emotional/relational nature (love, friendship, cherished identity) rather than merely physical ones. A middle section, 'Schools of Thought,' discusses rival philosophies and pedagogical schisms among sorcerous academies, both historical (First Age) and in the few that survive (such as one instructor's insistence on experiential, wilderness-based learning over traditional schooling). The chapter closes with 'The Heptagram,' describing the Realm's sole sanctioned school of magic on the Isle of Voices, secretly run by Sidereal Exalted using a Silurian pedagogical model. None of this material introduces mechanical player options (no new Charms, Backgrounds, Merits, or spells) -- it is pure flavor/setting context for how sorcery is learned and practiced.
notes: Chapter One: Magical Theory, pp. 9-19 (PDF 10-20), Savant and Sorcerer. Skimmed per this project's task instructions for 'rare player-facing content'; none was found. Documented as a single chapter-level excluded row rather than transcribed section-by-section, matching the precedent set for other lore-only chapters/sections in this project (e.g. book-of-bone-and-ebony-chapter-two-arcanoi-excluded).

name: Savant and Sorcerer, Chapter Four: Practical Summonings -- Storyteller/GM framework
summary: Chapter Four (printed pp. 71-99, PDF 72-100) is the procedural and Storyteller-facing framework for running demon and elemental summoning: binding oaths, task-based and mass-summoning rules, the Realm's licensing/pact system for elementals, and a full set of 'Limit Profile' archetypes (the Courtesan, Ecstatic, Functionary, Horror, Hunter, Killer, Slave, Vizier, Warden, Sufferer, etc.) giving each summoned servitor's Weakness, Limit conditions/tiers and Limit Break behavior. It supplies GM guidance for playing bound demons/elementals believably rather than new player-facing Charms, Backgrounds or spells -- the actual summoning spells a sorcerer casts are already catalogued separately as Chapter Five spells (e.g. commanding-the-beasts, summoning-the-lesser-minions-of-the-eyeless-face).
requirements: N/A -- GM-only procedural/NPC-behavior framework, not a player-facing power to gate behind a prerequisite.
mechanics: The chapter covers, in order: general principles of summoning and binding demons ('Cracks in the Demon Mind', 'In the Sorcerer's House', 'Binding Oaths', choosing and surviving a summoning, what happens on the summoner's death); elemental summoning and its social/political dimension (elemental snares, the Immaculate Philosophy's stance, the Realm's Celestial Hierarchy licensing system, long-term pacts, and an extended example organization, the Principality of the Shore, with its Wood Dragon Pact); task-based summoning, licensing/permissions and project planning for larger workings; mass summoning rules and Yozi possession; and a large 'Limit Profiles' section (roughly pp. 87-100/PDF 88-101) that gives ten major and several minor behavioral archetypes for bound creatures -- each with its own Weakness, three-tier Limit condition table (Low/Medium/High), a Limit Break effect, guidance on reducing Limit, and separate 'Practical Management' notes for demon versus elemental instances of that archetype. This is exactly parallel in structure to a Storyteller's guide for running NPCs realistically; none of it is a Charm, Background, Merit or spell a player character selects directly.
notes: Chapter Four: Practical Summonings, pp. 71-99 (PDF 72-100), Savant and Sorcerer. Skimmed per this project's task instructions for 'rare player-facing content'; the chapter turned out to be entirely Storyteller-facing summoning procedure and bound-creature behavioral guidance, so it is documented as a single chapter-level gm-only row rather than transcribed profile-by-profile, matching the precedent set for other large GM-facing frameworks in this project (e.g. necromancy-framework-and-circles' sibling exclusions and book-of-bone-and-ebony-chapter-two-arcanoi-excluded).

name: Selective Conception
summary: Characters with this Merit have full conscious control of their fertility: females can choose to conceive or not, and always know if they are pregnant. For an Abyssal, siring or bearing a child with a living lover carries a steep price -- it triggers 4 points of Resonance per this splat's own gaining-resonance rule.
mechanics: Characters with this Merit have full conscious control of their fertility. They may be as sexually active as desired and yet as fertile as always when they decide. Females with this Merit can automatically conceive as a result of a given union for a cost of one Willpower point, and such characters automatically know if they become pregnant. Males cannot assure conception and do not know if their sire offspring, but they may withhold their fertility as desired.
compatibility: Any character type, Exalted included; no splat-specific variant is given. Applies to Abyssals: deathknights are undead but retain fertility (per the Litany of Sins, siring or bearing a child with a living lover is itself a listed trigger for 4 points of Resonance), so this Merit remains meaningful for a deathknight who wants precise control over if/when that particular sin occurs.
notes: DERIVED FROM LUNAR'S VERIFIED PG TRANSCRIPTION (pg-merit-selective-conception): re-cited to the Players Guide directly rather than via Lunar's copy. No splat-specific eligibility restriction in the source text, so this Merit transfers to Abyssal characters without change. Abyssal-specific reinterpretation: this splat's own gaining-resonance row confirms deathknights can still sire or bear children with living lovers (a listed Litany of Sins trigger worth 4 Resonance), so Selective Conception remains mechanically relevant -- it lets a deathknight choose exactly when to risk that particular taint rather than leaving conception to chance.

name: Ambidextrous
summary: For one point, negates offhand penalties; the two-point ("omniambidextrous") version also lets the character hold weapons/tools with their feet as readily as their hands.
mechanics: For one point, the character can use both hands equally well and never suffers an offhand penalty for any task. Characters with the two-point version of this Merit can also hold weapons and tools with their feet as readily as their hands, an adaptation common among the Haltans of the East and highly useful for characters who have lost the use of both hands. Matters of balance and common sense still apply, however, so omniambidextrous characters will not be able to walk around carrying objects with every hand and foot simultaneously.
compatibility: Any character type; the source text grants a discounted 1-pt. cost for the two-point (omniambidextrous) version specifically to Lunar Exalted, which does not extend to Abyssal Exalted -- deathknights pay the full 2-pt. cost for that version.
notes: DERIVED FROM LUNAR'S VERIFIED PG TRANSCRIPTION (pg-merit-ambidextrous): re-cited to the Players Guide directly. The source text's discounted cost ("Lunars pay only one point to be omniambidextrous") is Lunar-specific and does not transfer to Abyssal; the closing discount sentence was dropped from this row's mechanics text since it does not apply here. Otherwise fully available to deathknights at the standard 1-/2-pt. cost.

name: Acute Sense
summary: One or more senses heightened to superhuman sensitivity; the 1-pt. version adds dice to Perception/Awareness rolls involving that sense but risks sensory overload, while the 3-pt. version grants preternatural acuity at the cost of being sensitive to other data.
mechanics: The character has one or more senses heightened to superhuman sensitivity, for a cost of one bonus point each. The character adds two dice to any Perception and/or Awareness dice pool involving a heightened sense, but his player must make a reflexive Wits + Awareness roll at standard difficulty whenever that sense experiences extremely intense stimuli. Failure inflicts a one-die penalty to all actions requiring concentration until the stimulus abates or the acclimation roll succeeds on a successive turn. If a character instead pays three bonus points per sense, the sense is heightened to preternatural acuity. Bonus points awarded by a heightened sense do not aid in resisting sensory-overload rolls.
compatibility: Any character type; no splat-specific variant is given. Fully applicable to Abyssal Exalted.
notes: DERIVED FROM LUNAR'S VERIFIED PG TRANSCRIPTION (pg-merit-acute-sense): re-cited to the Players Guide directly. No splat-specific eligibility restriction; transfers to Abyssal unchanged.

name: Double-Jointed
summary: Contortionist flexibility: the 1-pt. version adds a die to grappling/Athletics/Larceny rolls benefiting from flexibility; the 3-pt. version adds two dice and grants near-impossible feats of contortion.
mechanics: For a cost of one point, the character is unusually supple and capable of remarkable feats of contortion. Add one die to such an individual's grappling rolls, as well as to any Athletics or Larceny rolls where such flexibility proves advantageous. Characters with the three-point version of this Merit are uncanny contortionists, capable of seemingly impossible feats. These freakish acrobats add two dice to all rolls benefiting from flexibility and can bend every finger to the wrist, lock their legs straight up, maintain indefinite splits, dislocate and reset joints painlessly and slip free of most conventional restraints or a Dexterity + Athletics roll at a difficulty set by the Storyteller.
compatibility: Any character type; the source text grants Lunar Exalted a discounted 2-pt. cost for the greater version, which does not extend to Abyssal Exalted -- deathknights pay the full 3-pt. cost.
notes: DERIVED FROM LUNAR'S VERIFIED PG TRANSCRIPTION (pg-merit-double-jointed): re-cited to the Players Guide directly. The Lunar-specific discount sentence was dropped from this row's mechanics text since it names Lunar Exalted specifically and does not transfer to Abyssal.

name: Pain Tolerance
summary: Characters with this Merit can shrug off injuries that would leave most individuals unconscious or writhing in agony, at increasing tiers of pain-immunity and Awareness-roll cost. The source text calls this Merit "particularly common among ghosts and deathknights with corpse-like flesh" -- deathknights ARE Abyssal Exalted, making this one of this splat's most thematically-fitting Merits.
mechanics: Characters with this Merit can shrug off injuries that would leave most individuals unconscious or writhing in agony. For a cost of three points, but this increases the difficulty of any Awareness rolls based on touch by one. Five points allow the character to ignore two dice of wound penalties but also increase the difficulty of touch-based Awareness by like amount. The character feels nothing. Even if mortally wounded, he may continue to act without penalties for injuries that do not involve actual maiming. If maimed, the character can briefly jog on broken limbs, swing his shattered stump of an arm like a club and perform other acts of relentless torture. The downside to seven-point resilience is that the character automatically fails rolls that require a sense of touch and must visually inspect his body for injuries that require treatment to prevent infection or bleeding to death. The effects of Pain Tolerance are not cumulative with Charms and other magic that negate wound penalties. Only the most powerful effects apply. Pain Tolerance is particularly common among ghosts and deathknights with corpse-like flesh.
compatibility: Any character type; the source text names ghosts and deathknights (Abyssal Exalted) as being especially likely to have this Merit, owing to their corpse-like flesh. Directly and prominently applicable to Abyssal characters.
notes: DERIVED FROM LUNAR'S VERIFIED PG TRANSCRIPTION (pg-merit-pain-tolerance): re-cited to the Players Guide directly. HIGH ABYSSAL RELEVANCE: the source text's closing sentence explicitly names "deathknights with corpse-like flesh" as one of the two groups (alongside ghosts) for whom this Merit is particularly common -- deathknight is this splat's own in-fiction term for an Abyssal Exalt. No adaptation needed; this is one of the cleanest, most on-theme transfers from the Players Guide chapter.

name: Large Size
summary: Characters are roughly 25 percent (4-pt.) or nearly twice (6-pt.) larger than average, gaining bonus health levels but suffering a Dexterity penalty for fine manipulation at the higher tier.
mechanics: Characters with the four-point version of this Merit are roughly 25 percent larger than average, standing over seven feet tall and usually weighing in at 300 or more pounds. Such imposing bulk grants one additional -0 health level. For six points, the character is almost impossibly huge, standing eight to nine feet tall and weighing 500 or more pounds. Such characters receive one -0 level and one -1 level but lose one die from Dexterity rolls to use small weapons, writing instruments or other tools not designed for their massive hands. Unlike health levels bestowed by Charms, the added toughness afforded by this Merit is immediately evident to everyone. The character will certainly stand out in most crowds and may have to stoop to pass through doorways built for smaller individuals. Most characters have both Strength and Stamina rated at 3 or higher. Large Size may also represent obese characters of normal stature, particularly when coupled with a low Dexterity.
compatibility: Any character type; no splat-specific variant is given. Fully applicable to Abyssal Exalted, who do not shapechange the way Lunars do, so the source text's Lunar-only carryover-across-forms clause is not relevant here.
notes: DERIVED FROM LUNAR'S VERIFIED PG TRANSCRIPTION (pg-merit-large-size): re-cited to the Players Guide directly. The Lunar-specific clause about the bonus health level(s) carrying across all of a Lunar's shapechanged forms (and its Prey's Skin Disguise cross-reference) was dropped from this row's mechanics text -- Abyssal Exalted have a single fixed body and do not shapechange, so that clause has no Abyssal equivalent.

name: Legendary Attribute
summary: Grants the potential to raise a Physical (or, in other versions, Social or Mental) Attribute one dot higher than the normal Essence-based cap; all Exalted (including Abyssals) pay a reduced 3-pt. cost instead of the mortal 5-pt. cost.
mechanics: Characters with this Merit have the potential to attain superhuman strength, speed or resilience in which they can attain a rating one dot higher than the normal limit imposed by their Essence allows. This may be done during character creation or after. For mortals and Exalted with Essence 1 to 5, this allows a rating of 6 in the chosen Attribute. Exalted with Essence 6 may raise the Attribute to 7, etc. Other versions of this Merit exist to accommodate Social and Mental Attributes. Such Legendary Attributes follow the same rules apart from being classified as Social or Mental Merits.
compatibility: Any character type; all Exalted (Solar, Lunar, Sidereal, Abyssal, Dragon-Blooded, Alchemical) pay the reduced 3-pt. Exalted cost rather than the mortal 5-pt. cost. Abyssal Exalted qualify for this discount as Exalted.
notes: DERIVED FROM LUNAR'S VERIFIED PG TRANSCRIPTION (pg-merit-legendary-attribute): re-cited to the Players Guide directly. Cost is reduced to 3 points "for Exalted" generically (not naming any particular splat); Abyssals are Exalted and therefore qualify for the discount.

name: Special Resistance
summary: For every point invested, adds one die to Resistance/Endurance rolls versus poison or disease, or buys immunity to a specific poison/disease, or total immunity to all forms of injury for one point.
mechanics: For every point invested in this Merit, the character adds one die on applicable Resistance and Endurance rolls versus poison or disease. A character may not purchase more than five additional dice of either form of injury. Alternately, the character may have total immunity to a specific poison or disease for a cost of one point. The character will suffer no ill effects from that toxin or become sick from exposure to the malady. It is not possible to purchase immunity to infected wounds with this Merit. All forms of this Merit assume the character has built his Special Resistance through repeated exposure to the appropriate danger -- intentionally or otherwise.
compatibility: Any character type; no splat-specific variant is given. Fully applicable to Abyssal Exalted.
notes: DERIVED FROM LUNAR'S VERIFIED PG TRANSCRIPTION (pg-merit-special-resistance): re-cited to the Players Guide directly. No splat-specific eligibility restriction; transfers to Abyssal unchanged.

name: Special Sense
summary: One or more senses that process stimuli beyond the normal ranges for the character's species (e.g. heat vision, ultrasonic hearing, pheromone-like smell); no fixed mechanical effect, at Storyteller discretion, and stacks with Acute Sense.
mechanics: Characters with this Merit have one or more senses that process stimuli beyond the normal ranges for their species. For example, a character may be able to detect heat as well as visible light, to hear high frequency pitches like a dog or an uncapped Demesne. There is no fixed mechanical effect for this broader sensitivity, but Storytellers should certainly accommodate the character's gift when narrating sensory details. If this Merit is taken in conjunction with the appropriate Acute Sense Merit (see p. 18), the character's heightened awareness also applies to the unusual ranges of that sense. Every significant expansion of a single sense's range costs two bonus points.
compatibility: Any character type; explicitly stacks with the Acute Sense Merit.
notes: DERIVED FROM LUNAR'S VERIFIED PG TRANSCRIPTION (pg-merit-special-sense): re-cited to the Players Guide directly. The source text's "an especially pronounced Lunar Tell" flavor example was dropped from this row's mechanics text since it references a Lunar-only mechanic with no Abyssal equivalent; the remaining examples (heat vision, ultrasonic hearing, an uncapped Demesne) are splat-neutral and fully applicable to Abyssal characters.

name: Mutation
summary: Unusual, unnatural physical features from supernatural parentage, direct or ancestral exposure to the Wyld, or an uncapped Demesne; useful mutations are purchased as Merits, harmful ones as Flaws, and characters with an Essence pool may fuel activation costs with motes instead of Willpower.
mechanics: Characters with this Merit display unusual or unnatural features, typically as a result of supernatural parentage, direct or ancestral exposure to the Wyld or an uncapped Demesne. Regardless of their actual origin, aberrations purchased with this Trait take the form of Wyld mutations (see Exalted, pp. 280-281). Useful mutations require a number of bonus points equal to their mutation point rating + 2. Harmful mutations taken as Flaws grant bonus points equal to their mutation point rating + 1. Characters with an Essence pool may spend 2 motes of Essence to fuel any activation costs required by mutations but may not purchase Feats of Willpower under any circumstances. Similarly, a character with a natural healing rate superior to mortals cannot purchase the Regeneration affliction. As always, the Storyteller may veto or modify the cost of any mutation deemed unfair, particularly if that feature is already covered by another Trait. Features obtained from this Merit do not count as actual Wyld mutations for the purposes of determining whether a creature can safely endure Creation.
compatibility: Any character type; the core Exalted rulebook's mutation-point tables (pp. 280-281) are the relevant cross-reference for building these mutations. Available to Abyssal Exalted; the source text's flavor examples tied to Lunar-specific mechanics (an uncapped ancestral Wyld exposure or a pronounced Lunar Tell) and its cross-reference to Exalted: The Lunars' own extended mutation tables do not apply to this splat and were dropped.
notes: DERIVED FROM LUNAR'S VERIFIED PG TRANSCRIPTION (pg-merit-flaw-mutation): re-cited to the Players Guide directly. Abyssal-specific reinterpretation: the source text's "an especially pronounced Lunar Tell" flavor example and its direct cross-reference to Exalted: The Lunars pp. 212-225 were removed from this row's mechanics text, since neither has an Abyssal equivalent; the underlying Wyld-mutation framework (core Exalted pp. 280-281) is splat-neutral and applies to a deathknight the same as any other Exalt. A Storyteller running an Abyssal game could equally reflavor a mutation's in-fiction origin as necrotic taint from the Underworld or a Deathlord's own corrupting touch rather than Wyld exposure, at Storyteller discretion.

name: Common Sense
summary: A decent grasp of what constitutes a good idea, a bad idea and a very bad idea; won't rush into calamity without recognizing her folly.
mechanics: A character with this Merit has a decent grasp of what constitutes a good idea, a bad idea and a very bad idea. She won't rush into calamity without recognizing her folly, though nothing prevents her from ignoring her better judgment. This Merit chiefly exists to warn inexperienced players about the obvious dangers implicit in a particular course of action. The Storyteller should give fair warning in such cases, though he needn't belabor the point.
compatibility: Any character type; no splat-specific variant is given. Fully applicable to Abyssal Exalted.
notes: DERIVED FROM LUNAR'S VERIFIED PG TRANSCRIPTION (pg-merit-common-sense): re-cited to the Players Guide directly. No splat-specific eligibility restriction; transfers to Abyssal unchanged.

name: Internal Compass
summary: Uncanny sense of direction; gains one extra die to all rolls to navigate a ship or find her way through a maze, and can orient with regard to the cardinal directions of Creation OR THE UNDERWORLD.
mechanics: The character has an uncanny sense of direction and gains one extra die to all rolls to navigate a ship or find her way through a maze. She can orient herself with regard to the cardinal directions of Creation or the Underworld with a Wits + Awareness roll at standard difficulty.
compatibility: Any character type; no splat-specific variant is given. Particularly apt for Abyssal Exalted since the source text explicitly extends the orientation effect to the Underworld -- home turf for a deathknight navigating the Labyrinth and the shadowlands.
notes: DERIVED FROM LUNAR'S VERIFIED PG TRANSCRIPTION (pg-merit-internal-compass): re-cited to the Players Guide directly. No adaptation needed -- the source text already covers orientation "with regard to the cardinal directions of Creation or the Underworld," making this Merit a clean, ready-made fit for an Abyssal spending most of her time in the land of the dead.

name: Eidetic Recall
summary: Nearly perfect memory of everything witnessed, at a cost of one bonus point per sense the character can infallibly recall.
mechanics: Characters with this Merit have a nearly perfect memory of everything they have witnessed, at a cost of one bonus point for every sense the character can infallibly recall. It is assumed that this record is always functioning, though the Storyteller may require a Wits + Awareness roll to memorize and remember details observed in moments of intense stress (such as combat). Alchemical Exalted pay a flat cost of three points for full Eidetic Recall of all five senses.
compatibility: Any character type; Alchemical Exalted specifically pay a flat, discounted 3-pt. cost for the full (all five senses) version instead of the normal 5-pt. cost -- that discount does not extend to Abyssal Exalted, who pay the standard per-sense cost.
notes: DERIVED FROM LUNAR'S VERIFIED PG TRANSCRIPTION (pg-merit-eidetic-recall): re-cited to the Players Guide directly. The Alchemical-specific discount is retained in this row's compatibility text for reference (it does not apply to Abyssal) but was not folded into the cost field, matching how the Lunar row itself handled a discount naming a different splat.

name: Virtue Specialty
summary: Moral fortitude strengthened under specific conditions, adding dice to Virtue rolls equal to half the points invested when a specialty circumstance is invoked.
mechanics: A character with this Merit finds his moral resolve strengthened under certain conditions. For example, a meek villager may stand as a lion in defense of his family, and a celibate monk may train himself to better resist the lure of flesh. The character receives a number of additional dice to applicable Virtue rolls equal to half the number of points invested in this Merit. However, this also increases the difficulty where the Storyteller wishes to test against his moral judgment. Regardless of allocation and the number of times this Merit is purchased, a character may not have more than one specialty dice for a Virtue. This limitation duplicates the restrictions on specialties for Abilities. As always, Storytellers will veto any specialty deemed too broad.
compatibility: Any character type; no splat-specific variant is given. Applies to Abyssal Exalted through this splat's own Virtues of Death framework -- a deathknight's specialty condition is defined against her (redefined) Compassion/Conviction/Temperance/Valor the same way any other Exalt's would be, whether she is a loyal servant of her Deathlord or a renegade.
notes: DERIVED FROM LUNAR'S VERIFIED PG TRANSCRIPTION (pg-merit-virtue-specialty): re-cited to the Players Guide directly.
