summary: The 'Engines of Annihilation' system that 'allows characters and Storytellers to generate their own necromantic war machines from the ground up': choosing a frame material, a size class (1-4), optional weapon mounts and passenger capacity, an animation method (necromancy or nemissary piloting), defensive fortification, and offensive armaments, each step with its own Resources/Craft (Necrosurgery)/Essence costs.
requirements: Craft (Necrosurgery) at the tier matching the desired animation spell (•• for Walking War Machine, •••• for Spurring the Beast of War, ••••• for Incomparable Destruction Engine), the corresponding necromancy spell or the Nemissary's Ride/Drive the Necrotic Colossus Arcanoi, and the Resources costs listed per component below. Explicitly framed as usable by Abyssal Exalted directly: 'Those Abyssals who have mastered necrosurgery and Bone Graft Technique can use those abilities to assemble horrible necrotic concatenations... With enough time and resources, an Abyssal Exalt could use necrosurgery combined with Bone Graft Technique (and possibly Walking War Machine or its more powerful versions) to do any of the following...'
mechanics: FRAME: Humanoid (Resources: none) fuses/grafts human corpses; Animal (Resources: usually none, or the cost of a hunting party for exotic/Wyld-mutant/Dragon-Blooded specimens -- a war machine using Dragon-Blooded flesh for at least half its mass gains a bonus -1 health level) uses large animal or behemoth corpses; Bone (Resources none to ••• depending on rarity) anchors necromantic glyphs better than flesh; Metal (embellishments cost Resources per the Metal-by-Size-Class table below, doubled if metal forms the core structure) is fused in via the Abyssal Charm Bone Graft Technique; Necrotic Propulsion (Resources none to •) uses corpses or even single joints purely as motive power (rowers, cranks). SIZE CLASS: Class 1, Less Than Human (small drone-scale devices, cheapest and easiest to animate); Class 2, On a Human Scale (up to a large horse -- includes spine chains and the weapon of mephitic desolation); Class 3, Big and Dead (wagon to moderate-building scale, requires at least Spurring the Beast of War to animate); Class 4, Colossal (larger than a moderate building -- includes the thousand-corpse war frame, Juggernaut, and the web is the spider -- requires the Void Circle spell Incomparable Destruction Engine to animate). Metal-armor Resources cost by size class and metal (Iron •/••/••/•••; Jade or Soulsteel ••/•••/•••••/•••••; Brass/Steel •/••/•••/••• for Classes 1-4 respectively). WEAPON MOUNTS: Class 4-5 machines can mount First Age or Oblivion-based weapons for +• Resources. PASSENGERS: larger machines carry passengers/cargo (undead passengers pack far more densely than living ones). ANIMATION: Iron Reanimation (the necromancy spell Walking War Machine, already inventoried) needs Craft (Necrosurgery) ••, (8 - Essence) motes per necrosurgery success, one success per 100 lbs of flesh, animates up to a ton (Str 4/Dex 2/Sta 3/Per 2/Int 1/Wits 3, two -0/-1/-2 health levels per success); Onyx Reanimation (the Labyrinth Circle spell Spurring the Beast of War, see its own row) needs Craft (Necrosurgery) ••••, two days per roll (Str 6/Dex 2/Sta 5/Per 3/Int 1/Wits 4, two -0/-1, three -2 health levels per success); Obsidian Reanimation (the Void Circle spell Incomparable Destruction Engine, see its own row) needs Craft (Necrosurgery) •••••, three days per roll, minimum Essence cost equal to successes needed, doubled by the Storyteller for truly colossal machines (Str 8/Dex 3/Sta 7/Per 4/Int 2/Wits 4, three -0/-1, four -2 health levels per success). All three spell variants give the machine no functioning Virtues (auto-succeeds Valor, auto-fails everything else) and a base Initiative of 5/7/8 respectively. Nemissaries can animate a war machine instead of necromancy (via Nemissary's Ride or Drive the Necrotic Colossus), using the nemissary's own Mental/Social Attributes except Appearance, but many Deathlords distrust the technique since a nemissary retains her own free will. DEFENSE: a Vanguard of escorting zombies/war-body nemissaries protects slower machines; base health levels scale with size class and animating spell, and every 2 additional motes spent on toughness at creation grants (size class) -1 and (size class x 2) -2 health levels; armor plating grants Hardness/Soak by material (Bone 3/5L-6B/free; Iron 4/8L-8B/Resources = size class; Jade 7/14L-14B/size class x3; Soulsteel 9/18L-18B/size class x3); the ultra-rare Oblivion's Panoply plating (see its own row) is the strongest option. Repair requires an Intelligence + Craft (Necrosurgery) roll (three successes per health level lost to weekly wear-and-tear, at a rate of [size class] health levels lost per unrepaired week), the Abyssal Charm Form-Restoring Touch (doubled/tripled cost for size class 3/4 machines), or a nemissary's Instauration of the Fleshly Vessel. OFFENSE: Mechanical (built-in blades/hooks/crushing drums), Artifact (rare retrofitted First Age weapons, mostly unique to the First and Forsaken Lion), and Necromantic (weapons empowered by the Void Circle spell Oblivion's Avatar, see the necromantic-weaponry-oblivions-avatar-effects-menu row) are the three offensive categories.
cost: Highly variable by frame material, size class, animation spell, armor material and weapon mounts; see the Resources/Craft/Essence figures itemized in mechanics above.
compatibility: Framework/system text supporting the named war-machine catalog rows below (battle-snake, dread-brachial-sapping-array, thousand-corpse-war-frame, web-is-the-spider, weapon-of-mephitic-desolation, bone-spider-lotus, necro-drones-sample-catalog) plus the already-selectable bonestrider and the-insidious-ebon-xoanon rows.
notes: Chapter Four: Creations of Bone, 'Engines of Annihilation' through 'War Machines of the Dead' sections (Necrosurgery, Frame and Components, Size, Weapon Mounts, Passengers, Animation Options, Defense, Offense, Things Fall Apart), pp. 94-103 (PDF 95-104), Book of Bone and Ebony. Marked reference-only, matching this project's firm precedent for multi-step build-your-own systems (necromancy-framework-and-circles, hearthstone-formation-and-theme-rules, artifact-creation-framework-savant-and-sorcerer, warstrider-framework-and-rules) even though the source text explicitly frames this system as something 'characters' (not just Storytellers) use directly with concrete Craft/Resources/Essence costs -- 'selectable' in this project's schema is reserved for a single atomic, pick-able sheet item, not a combinatorial procedural system with dozens of interacting choices. The concrete named outputs of this framework (the two new necromancy spells, the Oblivion's Panoply material, and the individually named sample war machines below) are each broken out as their own rows with dispositions judged independently. Consolidated at framework granularity spanning multiple book subsections, matching the granularity already used for warstrider-framework-and-rules.

name: Oblivion's Panoply (Artifact •••••, scaling with Liege)
summary: The rarest and most effective war-machine armor plating: soulsteel soulforged personally by a Deathlord from a hekatonkhire's substance, lacquered to an obsidian sheen and sealed under a hair's-breadth layer of pure Oblivion that chills attackers, drains Essence on every hit, and nullifies physical force outright on its face (though its unarmored back has almost none of that protection).
requirements: Artifact •••••, plus one additional point of the Liege Background per five-foot-by-five-foot panel gained beyond the first, pending the character's Deathlord's (i.e. the Storyteller's) approval.
mechanics: Only characters with access to Void Circle Necromancy can even attempt to create Oblivion's Panoply, and it requires soulsteel forged from a hekatonkhire's own plasm -- extraordinarily rare even among the Deathlords' own hoards -- plus Resources ••••• in alchemical binding agents and 1 committed mote of Essence per five square feet created. No panel smaller than 25 square feet or thinner than two feet has ever been successfully made; smaller or irregular surfaces cannot hold the layer of Oblivion at all. Effects: Chill -- any attacker who successfully hits a panel must roll Stamina + Resistance (difficulty 2) or lose a point of Dexterity to numbness (orichalcum weapons insulate against this). Energy Drain -- every successful hit against the panoply with bare hands or non-orichalcum weapons drains the attacker of 5 motes of Essence (mortals instead age two years per hit); flames touching it are instantly extinguished, and water freezes and slides off. Force Nullification -- the face has an effective soak of 15L/20B, treated as hardened soak (ignoring all attacks whose raw damage is below that hardness); the unprotected back has only 2L/4B soak, so panels are always mounted with their backs shielded inside a soulsteel frame.
cost: Artifact ••••• (base access) plus one point of Liege per five-foot-by-five-foot panel beyond the first, subject to the character's Deathlord's approval; Resources ••••• in materials and 1 committed mote of Essence per five square feet to actually forge a panel.
compatibility: Used as war-machine armor plating; see war-machine-construction-framework's Defense/Armor subsection for how it compares to Bone/Iron/Jade/Soulsteel plating.
notes: Chapter Four: Creations of Bone, 'Oblivion's Panoply' sidebar, pp. 101-102 (PDF 102-103), Book of Bone and Ebony. Marked selectable rather than folded into the reference-only war-machine-construction-framework row: unlike that combinatorial system, this is a single named, discretely Artifact-and-Liege-gated material with its own fixed cost formula ('A character wishing to obtain panels of Oblivion's Panoply must have Artifact •••••. For every point of Liege he has on top of that, he may gain access to one five foot by five foot panel...'), directly analogous to how this project already treats other named Artifact-rated catalog items as selectable. The Deathlord-approval clause is preserved verbatim in requirements/cost since it is an explicit, concrete gating mechanic (GM sign-off keyed to an existing Background a PC already tracks), not an open-ended Storyteller-arbitrated process.

name: Spurring the Beast of War (aka Onyx Reanimation)
summary: Labyrinth Circle necromancy spell; the mid-tier war-machine animation spell, required to bring size class 3 ("Big and Dead") war machines to life, granting them stronger baseline Attributes/Abilities and more health levels per necrosurgery success than the entry-level Walking War Machine.
requirements: Necromancy: Labyrinth Circle (see Necromancy Framework and Circles); Craft (Necrosurgery) ••••.
mechanics: Also known among necromancers as Onyx Reanimation, this spell is the Labyrinth Circle's more powerful successor to Walking War Machine (Iron Reanimation), required to animate size class 3 war machines and usable for smaller ones as well. Each necrosurgery roll (an extended Intelligence + Craft [Necrosurgery] action) represents two full days of work, and casting the spell costs (8 - the necromancer's permanent Essence rating) motes per success rolled on that necrosurgery check. A war machine animated this way has: Strength 6, Dexterity 2, Stamina 5, Charisma 0, Manipulation 0, Appearance 0, Perception 3, Intelligence 1, Wits 4; no functioning Virtues (automatically succeeds on Valor rolls, automatically fails all others); Athletics 3, Awareness 2, Brawl 4, Dodge 4, Endurance 3, Melee 3, Resistance 3, Stealth 1; Base Initiative 7; soak highly variable by armor but never less than 4L/8B; and, per success on the initial necrosurgery roll, two -0, two -1 and three -2 health levels.
cost: (8 - the necromancer's permanent Essence rating) motes per success on the animating Craft (Necrosurgery) roll.
compatibility: Target: one war machine of size class 1-3 built via the war-machine-construction-framework; a nemissary may substitute Nemissary's Ride or Drive the Necrotic Colossus instead of this spell.
notes: Chapter Four: Creations of Bone, 'Animation Options' -> 'Necromancy' -> 'Onyx Reanimation' subsection, pp. 98-99 (PDF 99-100), Book of Bone and Ebony. Like oblivions-avatar, this spell appears inside Chapter Four's war-machine construction rules rather than Chapter Five's necromancy spell list, but it is mechanically a standard Labyrinth Circle Necromancy spell (the book's own 'By Way of Clarification' sidebar confirms 'Spurring the Beast of War is Labyrinth Circle Necromancy and is also known as Onyx Reanimation') and is filed here alongside this book's other necromancy spells for consistency.

name: Incomparable Destruction Engine (aka Obsidian Reanimation)
summary: Void Circle necromancy spell; the most powerful war-machine animation spell, required to bring size class 4 (colossal) war machines such as Juggernaut and the web is the spider to life, with the strongest baseline Attributes/Abilities and most health levels per necrosurgery success of the three animation spells.
requirements: Necromancy: Void Circle (see Necromancy Framework and Circles); Craft (Necrosurgery) •••••.
mechanics: Also known among necromancers as Obsidian Reanimation, this is the most powerful of the three war-machine animation spells and the only one capable of animating size class 4 (colossal) war machines. No necromancer can even attempt to cast it without Craft (Necrosurgery) •••••, and each necrosurgery roll represents three full days of work. The spell's minimum Essence cost equals the number of successes needed on the necrosurgery roll, which the Storyteller may double for truly colossal machines such as Juggernaut. A war machine animated this way has: Strength 8, Dexterity 3, Stamina 7, Charisma 0, Manipulation 0, Appearance 0, Perception 4, Intelligence 2, Wits 4; no functioning Virtues (automatically succeeds on Valor rolls, automatically fails all others); Athletics 4, Awareness 3, Brawl 6, Dodge 2, Endurance 4, Melee 4, Resistance 5, Stealth 1; Base Initiative 8; and, per success on the initial necrosurgery roll, three -0, three -1 and four -2 health levels.
cost: Minimum Essence equal to the number of successes needed on the animating Craft (Necrosurgery) roll (doubled at Storyteller discretion for colossal machines).
compatibility: Target: one war machine of size class 4 built via the war-machine-construction-framework.
notes: Chapter Four: Creations of Bone, 'Animation Options' -> 'Necromancy' -> 'Obsidian Reanimation' subsection, p. 99 (PDF 100), Book of Bone and Ebony. Like oblivions-avatar and spurring-the-beast-of-war, this spell appears inside Chapter Four's war-machine construction rules rather than Chapter Five's necromancy spell list, but it is mechanically a standard Void Circle Necromancy spell (the book's own 'By Way of Clarification' sidebar confirms 'Incomparable Destruction Engine is necromancy of the Void Circle and is also known as Obsidian Reanimation') and is filed here alongside this book's other necromancy spells for consistency.

name: Necromantic Weaponry: Sample Oblivion's Avatar Effects Menu
summary: A sidebar menu of 10 named necromantic-weapon effects a war machine can be granted by investing it with the Void Circle spell Oblivion's Avatar, ranging from cold/entropy damage auras to disease, bad luck, Strength drain, morale-breaking terror and Hearthstone-severing fields; these are not artifacts, and become inert if removed from the war machine they are bound into.
requirements: Requires the war machine to already be animated and then invested with the Void Circle spell Oblivion's Avatar (10 committed motes per power, or 40 motes and 5 experience points per power to make it permanent).
mechanics: Named sample effects: Chill of the Abyss (10-yard radius supernatural-ice-storm environmental damage, ongoing while Essence is invested); The Dread Black Beacon (50-yard radius black unlight reduces living visibility to foggy-night levels while granting the dead/Abyssals +1 die to attacks and materializing hungry ghosts regardless of time of day); Fortune's Inauspicious Nadir (100-yard radius bad-luck field raising the target number from 7 to 8, tens count as a single success); The Puissance-Arresting Eye (a 10-dice green-light beam attack that reduces a hit target's Strength to •, recovering one dot every two turns; Dodge-able, parry-able only with orichalcum, and negated entirely by Immunity to Everything Technique); The Rallying Chime of the Invincible Dead (Resources ••• add-on; a struck bell heals zombies, nemissary-possessed corpses, materialized ghosts and Abyssal Exalted within 20 yards one lethal health level per turn, but breaks permanently if removed from the war machine); Revealing the Well-Hidden Devils (30-yard black-fog field halves the Essence cost and waives the Willpower cost of Weighted With the Anchor of Flesh); Severing the Bond With Home (10-yard field disconnects Creation-based Hearthstones from their Manses for as long as a character remains inside it); The Softening Rains (once/day, 100-yard radius rust-rain instantly halves the soak of all non-Magical-Material armor); The Touch That Calls Them Home (100-yard radius forces a Stamina + Resistance roll at difficulty 5 or every wound the target has becomes infected); The Wailing Engine of Fear (50-yard radius Valor check at a two-die penalty, fleeing to the edge of the effect on failure or off the battlefield entirely on a botch). The weapon of mephitic desolation's disease/prayer-blocking effects are themselves cited as two applications of Oblivion's Avatar layered onto one war machine.
cost: N/A (menu of effects granted by casting oblivions-avatar on a war machine); The Rallying Chime of the Invincible Dead additionally costs Resources ••• to add to the war machine.
compatibility: Any war machine already animated via the war-machine-construction-framework; effects are lost if the necromantic weapon component is removed from its host war machine.
notes: Chapter Four: Creations of Bone, 'Necromantic Weaponry' sidebar, p. 109 (PDF 110), Book of Bone and Ebony. Catalogued as a single reference-only summary row at 'reasonable summary granularity,' matching the precedent set by warstrider-weapon-tables for large procedural weapon/effect menus, rather than 10 separate rows -- the source text itself frames these as flexible illustrative examples ('Storytellers are encouraged to come up with others as well') rather than a fixed catalog of discrete acquirable items.

name: Battle Snake (war-machine troop transport)
summary: A troop-transport war machine built from the mummified rib-segments of Seshasa, the two-mile-long Primal Basilisc slain in the First Age (or, in later builds, from cachalot/sea-dragon/behemoth ribs), each segment rigged with soulsteel hook-bands to carry the folded-up walking dead; a fully assembled 50-yard battle snake can transport 1,500 soldiers.
requirements: Deathlord-scale project: requires a source of enormous mummified ribs (Seshasa's remains, cachalot/sea-dragon/behemoth ribs, or Wyld-spawned monster remains) and necrosurgery to combine segments from different creatures.
mechanics: Each rib bears five soulsteel bands, each with three hooks holding a folded-fetal zombie or nemissary war body; a single rib carries up to 15 of the walking dead, a full segment (multiple ribs) 30, and a complete 50-yard, 50-segment battle snake up to 1,500 soldiers. Ghosts or deathknights can freely combine segments from different source creatures using necrosurgery, so a battle snake's length is limited only by available materials. Movement is a hybrid gliding/millipede motion that lets it cross terrain from Southern deserts to Northern ice equally well. Per the size-class stat table: Physical Attributes Strength 6/Dexterity 3/Stamina 5, no Willpower rating, Attack Speed 5/Accuracy 5/Damage 6B, Dodge/Soak 5, Abilities Athletics 3, Awareness 2, Brawl 4, Dodge 2, Endurance 3, Resistance 10, Stealth 1; each of the multiple body-segments has its own -0x2/-1x2/-2x3 health-level track.
cost: Resources/Craft costs per the war-machine-construction-framework's Frame (Animal/Bone) and Size Class rules; no separate Artifact rating is given.
compatibility: Size class 3 troop-transport war machine; carries walking-dead passengers per the war-machine-construction-framework's Passengers rule.
notes: Chapter Four: Creations of Bone, 'Battle Snakes' section and its stat-table entry, p. 107 (PDF 108, prose) and p. 111 (PDF 112, stat table), Book of Bone and Ebony. Marked reference-only, not selectable or gm-only: it is a generic, replicable transport-class template usable by 'ghosts or deathknights' with the right necrosurgery skill (not tied to one single Deathlord's unique property), but it is army-logistics infrastructure sized for hundreds-to-thousands of troops rather than a personal Artifact-rated item a single PC's sheet would track -- matching how the generic size-class stat table itself is presented as Storyteller/GM reference for running mass warfare, not a character-sheet purchase.

name: Dread Brachial Sapping Array (siege-tunneling war machine)
summary: A specialized siege engine of 50-100 severed arms joined at the shoulder, each finger tipped with an iron chisel via Bone Graft Technique, that claws slowly but relentlessly through earth or stone to tunnel beneath fortifications.
requirements: Bone Graft Technique (Abyssal Charm); the severed arms of 25-50 individuals; one success per five arms on the animating necrosurgery roll (via Walking War Machine).
mechanics: Digs through one yard of earth or one foot of stone per hour -- slow, but capable of tunneling through anything short of metal or the hardest basalt. Not effective in direct combat, though it can tear apart an unarmored mortal without much difficulty. Per the size-class stat table, health levels and soak depend on how many arms comprise the array (5-10 successes to create, granting 5-10 health levels); unarmored arrays have 1L/3B soak, armored (bracer-equivalent) arrays 3L/6B; Attack (Claw) Speed 4/Accuracy 5/Damage 4L, Defense 4, Abilities Athletics 1, Awareness 2, Brawl 2, Dodge 2, Endurance 1, Melee 2, Resistance 2, Stealth 1; the War Machine Exalted Power Combat table gives its claw a Dread Array Claw stat line of Speed 4/Accuracy 5/Damage 4Lp/Defense 5/Rate 1.
cost: Resources/Craft costs per the war-machine-construction-framework's Frame (Humanoid) and Size Class 2 rules; requires 25-50 severed arms as raw material.
compatibility: Size class 2 siege/tunneling war machine; animated by Walking War Machine.
notes: Chapter Four: Creations of Bone, 'Dread Brachial Sapping Array' section and its stat-table entry, p. 107 (PDF 108, prose) and p. 111 (PDF 112, stat table plus Exalted Power Combat claw stats), Book of Bone and Ebony. Marked reference-only for the same reasoning as battle-snake: a generic siege-engine template built via the standard construction framework, not an individually Artifact-rated personal possession.

name: The Thousand-Corpse War Frame (colossal troop-transport war machine)
summary: A colossal size class 4 troop transport and war machine: a bare 40-foot soulsteel skeleton that becomes a functioning giant only once over a thousand zombies swarm up its handholds and become its living (dead) musculature, straining in unison to flex each joint and take each 20-foot stride, crushing anything beneath its 10-foot disk feet for 30 bashing damage.
requirements: Built via the war-machine-construction-framework's Colossal (Size Class 4) rules; requires the Void Circle spell Incomparable Destruction Engine to animate the base frame, then roughly 1,000 zombies (100 at minimum for a slow non-combat walk) to crew it, directed by a nemissary stationed in its chest or head compartment.
mechanics: Loading takes a full hour; once mobile it walks with 20-foot strides. Its fist impacts can breach a stout castle wall, and its disk feet crush a 10-foot-diameter area for 30 levels of bashing damage. The lowest 10 feet of the frame is a layer of outward-facing zombies (often metal-plated for extra soak) that can attack anyone who approaches. Climbing it requires four successes on Strength + Athletics, imposes a -10 initiative penalty, and exposes the climber to five zombie attacks per turn at +2 dice; two or more successful Brawl attacks in a turn instead try to pull the climber into the writhing mass (-4 dice, -10 initiative, 10 zombie attacks per turn while trapped). A fall while climbing the front risks both falling damage and being trampled. As the war frame takes damage its Strength drops by 1 per 10 health levels lost; at Strength 0 it can no longer move and its remaining zombies scatter to fight individually. It may fight as a gestalt like a giant warstrider, or disperse its component zombies to attack separately once it reaches its destination.
cost: Resources/Craft costs per the war-machine-construction-framework's Size Class 4/Incomparable Destruction Engine rules, plus roughly 1,000 zombie crew (100 minimum).
compatibility: Size class 4 colossal war machine; the Mask of Winters' signature Juggernaut is explicitly a larger example of this same category of construction.
notes: Chapter Four: Creations of Bone, 'The Thousand-Corpse War Frame' section, pp. 104-106 (PDF 105-107), Book of Bone and Ebony. Marked reference-only: this is presented as a specific, singular named example (the Mask of Winters' Juggernaut is called out as a related but distinct, even larger construction) with a full monster-manual-style stat block and climbing/combat sub-rules, functioning as GM/setting reference for running Deathlord-scale siege warfare rather than a discretely Artifact-rated item a PC's own sheet would list.

name: The Web Is the Spider (colossal Essence-harvesting war machine)
summary: A colossal size class 4 war machine shaped like a vast 120-foot spider web of soulsteel and undead sinew, walking on eight 60-foot spoke-legs, that serves as portable bridge, siege ladder and living net while also draining blood from the wounded and dead through hollow soulsteel barbs to bank Essence for its ghost or Abyssal operators.
requirements: Built via the war-machine-construction-framework's Colossal (Size Class 4) rules; requires a soulsteel frame, sufficient Artifact rating for its eight Essence-containing gems, muscle and sinew from at least 60 corpses, and two successes per corpse used on an Intelligence + Craft (Necrosurgery) roll to assemble.
mechanics: Eight main 60-foot spokes radiate from a central hub and serve as legs; extending or contracting its component rods lets it double or halve its normal 120-foot diameter. Every intersection has a hollow soulsteel barb that exsanguinates the wounded or recently dead; for every two health levels of blood consumed, it banks 1 point of Essence in one of eight 60-mote Essence batteries at its hub. Ghosts or Abyssal Exalted may drain the stored Essence at a rate of 1 turn per 2 motes, except when a Deathlord personally rides into Creation, in which case the stored Essence is reserved solely for the Deathlord's use and poachers are severely punished.
cost: Resources for the soulsteel frame plus sufficient Artifact rating for the eight Essence-containing gems, per the war-machine-construction-framework's Size Class 4 rules; muscle/sinew from at least 60 corpses.
compatibility: Size class 4 colossal war machine; doubles as portable bridge, siege ladder, living net, and Essence-banking infrastructure for ghosts/Abyssals operating in Creation.
notes: Chapter Four: Creations of Bone, 'The Web Is the Spider' section and its stat-table entry, p. 107 (PDF 108, prose) and p. 111 (PDF 112, stat table -- Strength 8/Dexterity 3/Stamina 7, Attack [Leg Strike] Speed 5/Accuracy 9/Damage 12L, Defense 5/Soak 8L-10B, Dodge 2, gets two jabbing leg attacks per turn, and impaling for 5+ health levels forces a Stamina + Resistance roll or paralysis followed by ongoing Essence/blood drain), Book of Bone and Ebony. Marked reference-only: a labor-intensive, singular-scale Deathlord asset ('easily the equivalent of most First Age engines of war') presented as GM/setting reference rather than a personal Artifact purchase.

name: Weapon of Mephitic Desolation (atrocity-ritual war machine)
summary: A size class 2 war machine built by ritually murdering five children under age 10, stitching their harvested lungs into a bellows and their bodies into a singing circle animated by necromancy and Oblivion's Avatar, whose song spreads smallpox for half a mile and blocks all prayer in the area, risking divine retribution if played near a Gateway to Yu-Shan.
requirements: Necromancy (Walking War Machine or a stronger animation spell) plus the Void Circle spell Oblivion's Avatar (two applications, one for disease and one for prayer-blocking); five ritually slain children under age 10; five ghostly musicians (nemissaries will not do -- necromancy is specifically required for this construction) to possess the bodies and play them.
mechanics: Creation requires 10 successes on an extended Intelligence + Craft (Necrosurgery) roll (one roll per eight hours), then [(8 - the necromancer's Essence rating) x 10] motes to animate via Walking War Machine, plus the Essence cost of investing it with Oblivion's Avatar. Once played, its song exposes everyone within a half-mile radius to smallpox and raises the difficulty of all prayers (including prayer strips) in the area by three; all living spirits with Essence 3+ in the area suffer -5 dice to Perception. Playing it within 10 miles of a Gateway to Yu-Shan puts the Bureau of Humanity and the Division of Endings on immediate alert, with divine retribution a near certainty.
cost: Five ritually murdered children under age 10; 10 successes on an extended Craft (Necrosurgery) roll; [(8 - Essence) x 10] motes to animate; additional Essence to invest with Oblivion's Avatar (two applications).
compatibility: Size class 2 war machine; requires necromancy specifically (nemissary animation will not do).
notes: Chapter Four: Creations of Bone, 'Weapon of Mephitic Desolation' section and its stat-table entry, p. 108 (PDF 109, prose) and p. 111 (PDF 112, stat table -- Attack Speed -0/Accuracy -1/Damage -2, Soak 3L-6B, Abilities Performance 4; once it has taken half its health levels it can no longer sing), Book of Bone and Ebony. Marked gm-only rather than reference-only or selectable: this is an atrocity-ritual superweapon explicitly created by the Malfeans' own design intent, requiring the ritual murder of five children as a hard prerequisite with no player-facing acquisition path or Artifact/Background cost structure -- it is a Storyteller-side plot device/set piece (a weapon of mass destruction with in-fiction divine consequences attached), not something a player character commissions or builds as a normal crafting project even though it nominally has concrete Craft/Essence costs.

name: Bone Spider Lotus (armored troop-carrier war machine)
summary: A spider-shaped armored personnel carrier: a crude soulsteel disk mounted on eight rib-legs (or smaller segmented legs), capable of 70 mph for up to two weeks, with a toxic necrotic-jelly underbelly that shields and carries up to 20 zombies or nemissary war bodies (or half that as strike-platform weapon mounts, or twice as many necro-drones).
requirements: Built via the war-machine-construction-framework's Frame (Bone/Metal) and Size Class rules; five successes on a necrosurgery roll to build the standard version; animated by Walking War Machine.
mechanics: The necrotic-jelly underbelly grants 4L/10B soak to itself and its passengers in addition to their own soak. Fully loaded it carries 20 zombies or war-body nemissaries curled fetal, or 20 zombies' worth as up to twice that many necro-drones; configured as a strike platform/mobile weapon mount instead, it carries only 5 passengers but can mount First Age or necromantic weapons, whose effects stack if multiple weapons or platforms operate near one another. Per the stat table: Strength 6/Dexterity 3/Stamina 5, Attack Speed 7/Accuracy 5/Damage 6B or by mounted weapon type, Defense/Soak 4, Dodge 4, Abilities Athletics 3, Awareness 2, Brawl 4, Endurance 3, Resistance 10, Stealth 1.
cost: Resources/Craft costs per the war-machine-construction-framework's Frame and Size Class rules; five successes on the animating necrosurgery roll for a standard unit.
compatibility: Size class 3 troop-carrier war machine; carries zombies, nemissary war bodies, or necro-drones per the Passengers rule.
notes: Chapter Four: Creations of Bone, 'War Machines of the Dead' -> 'Bone Spider Lotus' section, pp. 111-112 (PDF 112-113), Book of Bone and Ebony. Marked reference-only for the same reasoning as battle-snake: a generic, replicable troop-carrier template presented as GM/setting reference for mass warfare, not a personal Artifact purchase.

name: Necro-Drones (sample size class 1-2 drone catalog)
summary: Small (size class 1, rarely 2) scavenger-built war machines assembled from a necrosurgeon's spare parts, used for reconnaissance, sabotage, and citadel guard/cleaning duty; five illustrative named samples are given, and Walking War Machine (or stronger spells) can animate them in swarms of 10-40 at once.
requirements: Built via the war-machine-construction-framework's Frame and Size Class 1 (rarely 2) rules; one to two successes on the animating necrosurgery roll (never more than five); alternatively piloted by a nemissary (via Nemissary's Ride), though that forgoes the higher Attributes/Abilities/health levels granted by the stronger necromancy spells.
mechanics: Sample named necro-drones given as illustrative examples: an animated dog's corpse with iron jaws (attack); a child's corpse with extra metal limbs sticking out of its back (attack); a head on a metal spider's body, animated by dead limbs (recon); a head with three sets of wings sutured to it (recon); blade burrowers, headless torsos augmented with extra flesh and metal limbs that burrow into the ground and leap out to attack approaching targets (attack); and two forearms fused together to form manacles (restraint). Necro-drones animated by Walking War Machine or nemissaries use the stats of a two- to four-segment spine chain; those raised with Spurring the Beast of War or Incomparable Destruction Engine use that spell's higher stats instead. Walking War Machine animates up to 10 drones at once, Spurring the Beast of War up to 20, and Incomparable Destruction Engine up to 40. A bone spider lotus can carry twice as many necro-drones as it carries zombies. Deathknights have been known to keep the least capable necro-drones as citadel guards and cleaning devices; under some circumstances they may be treated as extras.
cost: Resources/Craft costs per the war-machine-construction-framework's Size Class 1-2 rules; one to five successes on the animating necrosurgery roll.
compatibility: Size class 1 (rarely 2) drones, deployable from any troop carrier including bone-spider-lotus.
notes: Chapter Four: Creations of Bone, 'War Machines of the Dead' -> 'Necro-Drones' section, p. 110 (PDF 111), Book of Bone and Ebony. Catalogued as a single reference-only summary row at this project's usual 'reasonable summary granularity' rather than six separate rows, since the source text itself frames the six examples as flavor-only illustrations of an open-ended category ('Sample Necro-Drones') rather than a fixed, individually named catalog like the Warstrider classes.

name: Sky Eater (First and Forsaken Lion's transport airship)
summary: A shuriken-shaped flying troop transport, unique to the First and Forsaken Lion's Legion Sanguinary, formed by soulforging, Moliation and necrosurgery into a squat living hull whose dozens of screaming mouths inhale/exhale air for lift, carry up to 12 passengers at 80-120 mph, and can switch to a silent light-devouring stealth mode or a bone-grinding sonic attack mode.
requirements: Exclusive to the First and Forsaken Lion's forces; requires hundreds of ghosts painstakingly Moliated and soulforged together, plus (for operation in Creation) a manifestation engine.
mechanics: In flight mode, dozens of toothless mouths across the hull's top inhale the sky while mouths on the bottom exhale it, their tuned voices resonating like a choral drone; the vehicle carries up to 12 passengers (6 without crowding) at 80-120 mph. In stealth mode, the top mouths instead consume ambient light, rendering the ship silent and the sky above it pitch black while the bottom mouths exhale a faint black mist. In attack mode, hovering no more than 20 feet above a target, the bottom voices grow louder and shriller, grinding apart bones (and non-magical ceramic, stoneware and glass) beneath the ship. The First and Forsaken Lion has fitted some Sky Eaters with manifestation engines to let them operate in Creation.
cost: N/A -- a unique, hand-built Deathlord asset, not purchased via any standard Background.
compatibility: Deathlord-scale troop transport/attack airship, size class 4; requires a manifestation engine to function in Creation.
notes: Chapter Four: Creations of Bone, 'Airships' -> 'Sky Eater' section, pp. 112-113 (PDF 113-114), Book of Bone and Ebony. Marked gm-only, not reference-only: the text explicitly ties Sky Eaters to one specific Deathlord's forces ('the high-mobility transporters of the First and Forsaken Lion's army'), with no generic construction-cost breakdown given (unlike Battle Snake/Bone Spider Lotus/Dread Brachial Sapping Array, which are framed as generic templates any sufficiently skilled necrosurgeon could build) -- this is Storyteller-side setting/plot content for running that Deathlord's specific forces, not a replicable player-facing asset.

name: Maelstrom Barge (First and Forsaken Lion's mass-transport airship)
summary: A 50-yard pentagonal platform ringed with 10-30-foot rib-bone spars and soulsteel-mesh sails, invented by the First and Forsaken Lion to move up to 500 ghosts or 4-5 tons of cargo at up to 100 mph by summoning and riding a howling storm of pure Oblivion, whose passage causes Resonance-effect-like entropic fluctuations across the land below it.
requirements: Unique to the First and Forsaken Lion's invention/forces; a passenger must commit 15 motes of Essence to raise the driving storm.
mechanics: When a passenger commits 15 motes of Essence, howling Abyssal winds thick with spectres and flaying sand rise beneath the platform; unfurling its soulsteel-mesh sails between the horizontal spars lifts it airborne, stabilized by embedded Stability Charms. A fully laden barge triggers effects across a quarter-mile radius resembling 2-4-point Resonance manifestations (see Exalted: The Abyssals, p. 149); light loads are unlikely to trigger this. The barge is not combat-capable, but its raging winds add 4 to the difficulty of Archery/Thrown attacks made against those aboard, while storm-running boots or storm-warding parasols protect wearers from the storm's environmental effects (though not from the Archery/Thrown penalty or the black-miracle field). Over water the storms it leaves behind can rage for days after it passes; over land, the Underworld's own stability limits the storm to the barge's immediate passage. Anyone caught in the storm takes damage as a supernatural ice storm, resisted with a difficulty 3 (land) or difficulty 5 (Sea of Shadows) Intelligence + Survival roll.
cost: N/A -- a unique, hand-built Deathlord asset; operating it costs 15 motes of committed Essence per flight.
compatibility: Deathlord-scale mass-transport airship, size class 4; not combat-capable.
notes: Chapter Four: Creations of Bone, 'Airships' -> 'Maelstrom Barge' section (including the 'Soulsteel Mesh' and 'Oblivion's Terrible Wake' sidebars), pp. 113-114 (PDF 114-115), Book of Bone and Ebony. Marked gm-only for the same reasoning as sky-eater: explicitly a singular Deathlord-invented asset ('The Deathlord transformed... the First and Forsaken Lion came up with the notion...'), not a generic buildable template. The Soulsteel Mesh sidebar (bashing soak 30/lethal soak 15, nets count as Artifact ••••, chain swathing needs Resources/Artifact •••••) and Oblivion's Terrible Wake sidebar (mechanical detail for the storm's damage/resistance rolls) are folded into this row's mechanics/notes rather than split out, since both are scoped narrowly to explaining the barge's own storm effect.

name: The Final Maelstrom (First and Forsaken Lion's unfinished flagship, plot hook)
summary: A singular, still-unfinished superweapon: the First and Forsaken Lion's secret flagship project, three times the length of the Mask of Winters' Juggernaut, built from the hollow carapace of a dead behemoth plated in jade and soulsteel to tap Underworld power even in Creation, nearing completion after nearly a century of construction and hidden even from the other Deathlords.
requirements: Sole property of the First and Forsaken Lion; not a purchasable or player-facing asset under any Background.
mechanics: Commissioned by the First and Forsaken Lion nearly a century before publication, originally not expected to complete for decades more, but now (per the Deathlord's own optimistic estimate, aided by his deathknights' skilled labor) nine years or less from completion. When finished it will bristle with pyre-flame lances and entropic implosion bows, though the Lion intends to use it as one piece of an integrated strategy (alongside his warstriders and the Legion Sanguinary's ground forces) rather than as a crutch. It remains a secret even from the other Deathlords.
cost: N/A -- unique, unfinished, and never framed as purchasable; pure plot/setting content.
compatibility: Not yet operational as of this book's writing; a Storyteller-facing future plot hook, not a currently usable asset.
notes: Chapter Four: Creations of Bone, 'Airships' -> 'Final Maelstrom' section (and the adjoining 'The Gravest Threat' sidebar profiling the First and Forsaken Lion himself), pp. 114-115 (PDF 115-116), Book of Bone and Ebony. Marked gm-only: this is explicitly incomplete, secret-even-from-other-Deathlords narrative plot content with no player-facing mechanics, cost structure, or acquisition path whatsoever -- a pure Storyteller campaign hook for a future reveal, the clearest possible case for this disposition in the whole chapter.

name: Armies of the Dead: Troop Types and Battlefield Logistics
summary: Chapter Four's opening section on how the Deathlords field zombies, ghosts, hungry ghosts and Moliated ghosts as mass-army troop types, including Battlefield Support Labs and Resurrection Pits (Artifact-rated field infrastructure that reclaims 20-40% of destroyed zombies as reassembled 'composite zombies'), zombie-borne disease mechanics, and the catapult-launched 'Storm of Hungry Ghosts' siege tactic.
requirements: N/A -- Storyteller-facing overview of Deathlord army composition and siege tactics, not a player-selectable option.
mechanics: Zombies are the Deathlords' preferred disposable shock troops (cheap, disease-bearing, but they never heal); wounds a zombie inflicts require five successes on a Stamina + Resistance roll to resist infection (versus the normal difficulty-3, three-success threshold for ordinary battlefield wounds), reduced to a difficulty-2 roll if the wound is sterilized with fire or alcohol within minutes (fire damage used this way counts as one level of lethal damage). Battlefield Support Labs are mobile necrosurgery teams that recover 10 health levels' worth of intact zombie flesh and stitch it into 'meat golems,' requiring five successes on an Intelligence + Craft (Necrosurgery) extended roll (one roll per hour) and then a 24-hour soak in a Resurrection Pit (a Hearthstone •••+ or soulfire-crystal-powered soulsteel cylinder, Artifact •••• holding ~20 meat golems or Artifact ••••• holding ~60, Resources •• to maintain, functional only in the Underworld/shadowlands) to fuse and reanimate; this reclaims 20-40% of a force's zombie casualties without needing a dedicated necromancer. Ghosts play a smaller army role than zombies/hungry ghosts (materializing costs nearly half a ghost's Essence pool), but war-ghost garrisons ambush effectively in shadowlands at night. Hungry ghosts are naturally material at night at no Essence cost, and 'strategic violation' of a slain mortal's corpse yields both a zombie and a hungry ghost from one body; the Shade Prison Amulet spell lets sieging forces catapult-launch swarms of captured hungry ghosts into besieged cities as 'ghost boulders.' Moliated ghosts (via the Shifting Ghost-Clay Path Arcanoi) can add battlefield mutations beyond the core book's list -- Huge Size (+2 -2 health levels), Maw (Str+4L bite), Prehensile Tail, Spikes (3L to anyone landing a hand-to-hand hit), and Suckers (+4 dice on clinch attacks) -- or a possessed mortal can manifest Ghost-Devil Form covertly via Puppeteer's Masterful Hand.
cost: N/A (army-composition/tactics overview); Battlefield Support Labs/Resurrection Pits are Artifact •••• or ••••• field infrastructure, Resources •• to maintain.
compatibility: Deathlord-army-scale content; relevant to a character with the Abyssal Command Background who commands large troop formations, but not itself a Background purchase.
notes: Chapter Four: Creations of Bone, 'Armies of the Dead' through 'Moliated Ghosts' sections (Zombies, Battlefield Support Labs, Zombies and Mortals, Disease, Ghosts, A Storm of Hungry Ghosts, Moliated Ghosts), pp. 81-87 (PDF 82-88), Book of Bone and Ebony. This is the remainder of the chapter's resume-point scope that precedes the nemissary/Custom Corpses material; marked gm-only as Storyteller-facing mass-warfare/tactics content (matching the precedent set by savant-and-sorcerer-chapter-four-practical-summonings-gm-only for similarly narrative/procedural GM content), with its two genuinely player-relevant mechanical carve-outs broken into their own rows: mortal-ally-and-command-amulets (concrete Artifact/Resources-costed items) and the-zenith-problem (a combat mechanic directly affecting Abyssal PCs). The Moliated Ghosts' Shifting Ghost-Clay Path mutations are ghost Arcanoi, excluded for the same reason as book-of-bone-and-ebony-nemissary-arcanoi-excluded and book-of-bone-and-ebony-chapter-two-arcanoi-excluded.

name: Mortal Ally and Command Amulets (Soul Brand variant / Black Investiture)
summary: Two implantable amulets a necromancer can craft to integrate living mortal troops into an army of the dead: a 30-mote Soul Brand variant that marks a mortal as inedible/friendly to the undead, and a 40-mote-plus-1-Willpower Black Investiture amulet that additionally grants the wearer limited command over zombies, obtainable via Artifact •••, Backing (Deathlord) ••-••••, or Resources ••••.
requirements: Knowledge of the Shadowlands Circle spell Soul Brand (for the ally variant) or the 20-mote Labyrinth Circle spell Black Investiture (for the command variant); Artifact •• (ally amulet) or Artifact •••/Backing (Deathlord) ••/Resources •••• (command amulet) to acquire one.
mechanics: The ally variant is a more expensive Soul Brand casting (30 motes) that produces an amulet or subdermally implanted talisman identifying a mortal as an inedible ally to the undead; implanted versions cannot be lost, while portable ones are deliberately kept rare due to the risk of loss/theft. These count as level-2 artifacts, last indefinitely in the Underworld/shadowlands but disintegrate after a year in Creation, and are destroyed instantly by Sapphire Countermagic; they can also be issued to characters with Backing (Deathlord) •• or bought on the black market for Resources ••••. The command variant instead uses the 20-mote Labyrinth Circle spell Black Investiture, layered on top of Soul Brand's ally effect, to grant the mortal wearer limited authority to command zombies as a lieutenant; committing it to an amulet costs 40 motes and 1 Willpower and requires the caster to commit 1 mote of Essence to the amulet (reflexively withdrawable by the caster at any time to instantly de-authorize a turncoat mortal). Nemissaries sometimes use these amulets too, at the same Artifact •••/Backing ••••/Resources ••••• cost tiers.
cost: Ally amulet: 30 motes to cast, Artifact ••, or Resources •••• (black market). Command amulet: 40 motes + 1 Willpower to cast (plus 1 committed mote of Essence), Artifact •••, Backing (Deathlord) ••, or Resources ••••; ••••/••••• tiers respectively if issued to a nemissary instead.
compatibility: Worn by mortal troops integrated into a Deathlord's army; the command variant additionally usable by nemissaries.
notes: Chapter Four: Creations of Bone, 'Zombies and Mortals' section, pp. 83-84 (PDF 84-85), Book of Bone and Ebony. Marked selectable, unlike the surrounding armies-of-the-dead-overview-and-logistics row: these are concrete Artifact/Resources-rated items with fixed costs, matching the precedent set by stomach-weighting-powder and bindings-of-eternal-preservation for individually purchasable equipment, even though this equipment is typically worn by NPC mortal followers rather than the Abyssal PC personally.

name: The Zenith Problem (Solar Zenith anima flare vs. the undead and war machines)
summary: A sidebar detailing why Zenith Caste Solars are the Deathlords' most feared enemies: their anima powers can pull ghosts (and mortwights) straight into Lethe, incinerate corpses before necrosurgeons can harvest them, paralyze/repel the walking dead within a radius, and directly damage undead troops, war machines, and even deathknights -- resistible only via an Essence roll (deathknights/Deathlords/Infernals) or the Void Circle spell Abyssal Aegis (full immunity).
requirements: N/A -- this is a hazard/threat mechanic imposed by an enemy Zenith Caste Solar's anima powers, not a purchasable option; the Abyssal Aegis counter-spell is the row's one actionable player-facing takeaway.
mechanics: A Zenith's touch-based anima flare can consecrate a ghost's remains to the Unconquered Sun, forcing the ghost's player to roll Willpower (difficulty 7, -1 per point of the ghost's permanent Essence, +1 die per two dots of Fetters) or be pulled instantly and permanently into Lethe; the same flare destroys walking-dead corpses outright, denying necrosurgeons the raw material to harvest them. In its Dawn-anima-flare-style incarnation (usable only against undead/demons/creatures of darkness), zombies auto-succeed their Valor rolls but still cannot approach within the Zenith's Essence rating in yards, falling inert if they enter that radius anyway, and the anima flare inflicts grievous automatic damage on ghosts/hungry ghosts/walking dead/Abyssals alike, destroying undead extras outright. Only deathknights, Deathlords and Infernal Exalted can resist it, by spending 5 motes and rolling permanent Essence (reflexively; each success cancels one Zenith success). A nemissary possessing a host body takes at most one level of damage personally, with any excess falling on the host corpse instead; a ghost/demon possessing a living body instead takes one bashing level itself while the invading spirit eats the rest as aggravated damage. Any war machine that is undead-flesh-based, necromantically animated, or fueled by soulfire crystals/Essence gems/an Underworld Hearthstone takes full damage from the flare (soulsteel components remain invulnerable but 'shriek in agony'). The Void Circle spell Abyssal Aegis grants total immunity to the Zenith anima flare, and the First and Forsaken Lion's own armor is confirmed to carry this enchantment.
cost: Resisting as a deathknight/Deathlord/Infernal: 5 motes of Essence, reflexive action, roll permanent Essence.
compatibility: Directly relevant to Abyssal PCs, their nemissary/ghost allies, and any war machines they control when facing a Zenith Caste Solar antagonist.
notes: Chapter Four: Creations of Bone, 'The Zenith Problem' sidebar, p. 85 (PDF 86), Book of Bone and Ebony. Marked reference-only rather than selectable: this documents an enemy threat/hazard mechanic and its one counter (Abyssal Aegis, already an existing selectable spell row) rather than a purchasable Background/Artifact/Charm of its own, matching how comparable hazard-mechanic sidebars elsewhere in this inventory (e.g. disease rules folded into armies-of-the-dead-overview-and-logistics) are catalogued as reference material rather than selectable items.

name: Ghost Cestus (Artifact •••)
summary: Universal cross-splat artifact: an armored fighting glove (cestus) enchanted with orichalcum, moonsilver, starstone, or (most commonly) jade so its punches and grapples can strike and subdue spirits, ghosts, and gods who are normally untouchable to mortal fists.
requirements: None (usable by mortals, magicians, sorcerers, or any Exalt without special training).
mechanics: Ghost cesti work against umbrood and ghosts just as well as against normal humans, requiring no special training to use. When a character fights using ghost cesti, the player makes all the normal dice rolls for unarmed combat and inflicts the normal, Strength-based damage of the combat maneuver, but instead of health levels, the character inflicts points of temporary Willpower loss on the spirit target (see Exalted core rulebook p. 147 for the total effects of Willpower loss on spirits/humans). The victim can soak this attack using her own Willpower. Spirits reduced to 0 Willpower this way become totally obedient to whoever subdued them. Spirits and mortals both recover lost Willpower from this effect as if it were bashing damage. Ghost cesti cannot outright kill a spirit -- that requires more dreadful and powerful magic -- but a cestus-wielding warrior or wizard can pummel even a powerful spirit into submission, since spirits are unused to taking uppercuts from 'mere mortals.'
compatibility: Any wielder (mortal, magician, sorcerer, or Exalt of any splat, including Abyssals); a local spirit challenged the Empress's authority once and she sent a champion armed with ghost cesti to subdue it, and non-Exalted priests of the Immaculate Order also carry ghost cesti.
notes: DERIVED FROM LUNAR'S VERIFIED TRANSCRIPTION (artifact-ghost-cestus): re-cited to Exalted Storyteller's Companion directly, no independent re-read. Chapter Four: Further Wonders, 'Ghost Cestus (Artifact •••)', printed pp. 77-78 (PDF 78-79), is a universal cross-splat artifact catalog, not restricted to any splat (per the project owner's brief), so this row is included verbatim for Abyssal with no compatibility caveats to adapt -- Lunar's own transcription notes it was recorded as the master copy for exactly this kind of downstream derivation.

name: Sling Bow of Ice (Artifact •••)
summary: Universal cross-splat artifact: a bow-and-sling hybrid weapon common in the First Age, made of mingled black and blue jade, that fires bullets or bolts which explode on impact into a cloud of snow and shivering, uncontrollable cold, freezing the ground and everyone nearby.
requirements: An Essence-manipulating wielder (the weapon itself is inert in the hands of a mortal with no Essence to fuel it).
mechanics: A sling bow resembles a normal bow, but instead of arrows it fires bullets of stone or metal, or a sling. These particular sling bows are fashioned of mingled black and blue jade carved with a fine tracery of frost ferns. A bolt of black or blue jade fired from the weapon explodes on impact into a cloud of snow and ice that sets everyone within 20 feet shivering uncontrollably, no matter how warmly they are dressed, unless they carry a bit of orichalcum or are protected by magic that shields them from cold. It also coats the ground with a thin layer of slippery ice, making it hard to remain upright. The Sling Bow requires a single mote of Essence to fuel its magic; the wielder rolls Essence + Archery. For each success, everyone within 10 feet of the impact loses one dot of Dexterity from frostbitten numbness and slipping on the icy ground; a character reduced to 0 Dexterity can do nothing but huddle in misery. A character's Essence is subtracted from the number of successes rolled. The supernatural cold lasts one turn per success rolled in mild weather, and five minutes per success if the weather is already chill. Anyone who enters the zone regains Dexterity per turn; anyone who leaves it regains Dexterity per turn. A character may soak the cold using her Essence rating; the weapon does not affect Undead at all. A person who carries a bit of orichalcum, or characters with charms or spells that protect them from extreme cold, become immune to the effect. In the First Age, soldiers operating alongside Sling Bow-armed Exalted wore orichalcum rings to protect themselves from the weapon's effect; since the art of forging orichalcum was lost centuries ago, latter-day warriors must exercise care when employing the Bow.
compatibility: Any Essence-manipulating wielder (any Exalt, sorcerer, or Essence-wielding magician, including Abyssals); historically used by General Tepet Hala in the Great Eastern War, where it drove the Eastern Army across a river and let him take the enemy army by surprise. The weapon 'does not affect Undead at all,' which is a targeting-immunity note about the frost effect's victims, not a restriction on who may wield it -- an Abyssal wielder simply cannot use it against undead targets (including other deathknights, ghosts, or her own zombie troops), but suffers no restriction firing it at the living.
notes: DERIVED FROM LUNAR'S VERIFIED TRANSCRIPTION (artifact-sling-bow-of-ice): re-cited to Exalted Storyteller's Companion directly, no independent re-read. Chapter Four: Further Wonders, 'Sling Bow of Ice (Artifact •••)', printed p. 78 (PDF 79), is a universal cross-splat artifact catalog entry. Flagged the 'does not affect Undead' clause in compatibility since an Abyssal is an undead Exalt herself, but the clause describes the frost effect's target immunity (Undead targets are unaffected by the cold), not a splat-based wielder restriction, so the row remains selectable rather than excluded.

name: The Golden Viper (Artifact •••••)
summary: Universal cross-splat artifact: a First Age automaton shaped like a six-foot orichalcum-and-jewel serpent, intelligent enough to speak and advise its owner, that serves whoever possesses it and can transmute a bite victim's flesh into gold.
requirements: Ownership of the Viper following the death of its previous owner (it serves anyone who possesses it once its prior master has died).
mechanics: The Golden Viper is the most intelligent automaton known, and even First Age texts speak of it as a notable relic. This lifelike serpent, fashioned of orichalcum and jewels in a framework of starstone, stretches six feet long and is about four inches thick at its thickest. The Viper serves anyone who possesses it once its previous owner is dead. The Viper is a formidable assassin: it can move through small openings and strikes like a real serpent, coiling and lashing out. In a matter of seconds, a person bitten by the Viper turns to gold (ordinary gold, not orichalcum). Magicians and Exalted have somewhat greater resistance to the Viper's bite than do more mortal folk, but even they can be slain and transmuted. The automaton knows whatever any of its clients knew; it advises its owner on the basis of this truly awesome base of stolen knowledge and experience. The Golden Viper knows no mercy or compassion; it advises the most ruthlessly practical course whatever goal its master seeks. If the Viper's master is not already a complete cynic by human nature, she will after a few years of the Viper's callous insight into human foibles. System: Attributes: Strength 3, Stamina 5, Perception 5, Intelligence 7, Wits 5, Charisma 3, Manipulation 5, Appearance 3, Willpower 10. It lacks Virtues since these have no meaning for its cold, inhuman intellect. Instead of a list of specific Abilities, the Storyteller may assume that it has a rating of 4 in any Ability it needs, with one exception: it remembers nothing about the First Age -- or claims not to. It speaks all known languages, and rapidly learns any new one it is exposed to. Its bite inflicts a base of 6L special damage; only armor can soak this damage, though Exalted can add their Essence to their soak rating. Each health level inflicted also strips away one point of Dexterity, as the victim stiffens, and it has a soak of 7L/10B. Its health levels are -0x3/-1x2/-2x2/-4x2/Incap x3. Restoring a health level lost to the Golden Viper is a difficulty 2 task on an Intelligence + Crafts roll.
compatibility: Any owner who acquires it after its previous owner's death, of any splat including Abyssals; functions as an autonomous intelligent servant/assassin rather than a wielded or attuned item.
notes: DERIVED FROM LUNAR'S VERIFIED TRANSCRIPTION (artifact-the-golden-viper): re-cited to Exalted Storyteller's Companion directly, no independent re-read. Chapter Four: Further Wonders, 'The Golden Viper (Artifact •••••)', printed p. 78 (PDF 79), is a universal cross-splat artifact catalog entry with no splat-restricting language of any kind -- included verbatim.

name: Land Ship (Artifact •••••)
summary: Universal cross-splat artifact: an extremely rare First Age vessel with a keel of interleaved yellow and black jade that lets it sail across dry land as if it were water, powered by an Essence-manipulating captain and crew.
requirements: An Essence-manipulating captain to sail it (First Age devices existed that stored Essence so a land ship could sail without an Exalted crew, but these devices have all been lost or destroyed).
mechanics: In the First Age, land ships were common. Very few of them remain -- masters of earth and water magic, working together, could craft new land ships, but this has not happened in centuries. Although land ships were once rare, war or accident has destroyed most of them; two Dragon-Blooded nobles own land ships, so does one Deathlord, and perhaps a few more await discovery. All the magic of a land ship rests in its keel -- a long, curving strip of yellow jade sandwiched between strips of black jade. The rest of the ship is ordinary wood and metal, built however the shipwright pleased, and subject to normal wear and aging. The two land ships in mortal hands are both single-masted forty-footers with high prows, one square-rigged and the other lateen-rigged; the Deathlord's ship is a 60-foot sloop. System: A land ship requires someone who can manipulate Essence to start it sailing on land, though in the First Age there were devices that contained Essence that could be used so that the vessels did not need Exalted crews. To start the vessel sailing requires one mote of Essence per hour and a simple success on an Essence + Sailing roll. With a good wind and a skilled crew, a land ship can sail 10 miles per hour, +1 mph for each success on the captain's Intelligence + Sailing roll -- wind permitting. Bad weather or obstacles such as trees or boulders result in increased difficulty. A land ship's magic has its limits: a land ship cannot sail up or down cliffs, any more than a mundane ship can sail up or down a waterfall. The one time someone tried using a land ship to breach castle walls, the ship's high prow went into the wall -- and the liquefied stone pushed the ship down into the earth. The land ship sank into the earth.
cost: 1 mote per hour of sailing (plus an Essence + Sailing roll to begin)
compatibility: Any Essence-manipulating captain (any Exalt, sorcerer, or Essence-wielding pilot, including Abyssals); currently known to be owned by two Dragon-Blooded noble houses and ONE DEATHLORD -- this is one of the few universal-catalog artifacts with a documented owner among the Deathlords themselves, directly relevant to Abyssal Backing/Liege play.
notes: DERIVED FROM LUNAR'S VERIFIED TRANSCRIPTION (artifact-land-ship): re-cited to Exalted Storyteller's Companion directly, no independent re-read. Chapter Four: Further Wonders, 'Land Ship (Artifact •••••)', printed p. 79 (PDF 80), is a universal cross-splat artifact catalog entry; the source text itself notes one of the three known surviving land ships is already owned by a Deathlord, making this entry especially on-theme for Abyssal.

name: Singing Staff (Artifact ••••)
summary: Universal cross-splat artifact: a man-high staff of white jade, played with a rosined bow like a musical saw, that reshapes earth, sand, clay, or stone into whatever form its music evokes -- as useful for digging canals as for toppling castle walls.
requirements: An Essence-manipulating player skilled in Performance (even in the First Age, a Singing Staff required an Exalted wielder).
mechanics: The Singing Staff demonstrates the odd approach to magic taken by some First Age magicians. This man-high staff of white jade is carved in an irregular series of waves and swellings, with a knob at each end. When rubbed with a rosined bow, the Singing Staff emits a tone, like a musical saw; different parts of the staff play different pitches and timbres. If one plants the end of the Staff on the ground and plays it correctly, the land responds to the music, rising and falling like waves or shaping itself like clay molded by unseen hands. This makes the Singing Staff precious as both a tool and a weapon: the Staff's uses are limited only by the skill of its player. Singing Staves are immensely sophisticated devices, despite their simple appearance. They were never easy to make, and in the modern era are vastly more difficult -- only three are known to exist: one is in the hands of the Empress and stored among her personal effects, one is held by the Immaculates of Paisep for study, and one was lost in battle with the Tepet legions and now lies on the bottom of the Inner Sea. Although the effects of the Staves are functionally identical, each has its own musical 'tuning.' System: Wielding the Staff's magic costs one mote of Essence per turn, and even in the First Age required an Exalted wielder. Each turn of use, the Staff can reshape 100 cubic feet of earth, sand, or clay, or 20 cubic feet of stone. To use the Staff, the character's player must succeed on an Essence + Performance roll (difficulty set by the detail or magnitude of the task). The Storyteller may demand multiple rolls to succeed at lengthy tasks, or additional Ability rolls for tasks that demand specialized training. For instance, constructing an ornamental stone pavilion might require three Essence + Ability rolls to use the Staff correctly, plus another Craft roll to get the ornamental carving right.
compatibility: Any Essence-manipulating wielder with Performance skill, of any splat including Abyssals; the three known Staves are held by the Empress, the Immaculate Order (for study), and one was lost when the Tepet legions were defeated and now rests at the bottom of the Inner Sea.
notes: DERIVED FROM LUNAR'S VERIFIED TRANSCRIPTION (artifact-singing-staff): re-cited to Exalted Storyteller's Companion directly, no independent re-read. Chapter Four: Further Wonders, 'Singing Staff (Artifact ••••)', printed pp. 79-80 (PDF 80-81), is a universal cross-splat artifact catalog entry. 'Paisep' transcribed as printed per Lunar's own row, which flags the place name as difficult to make out on the scanned page.

name: Eye of Autochthon (Artifact N/A)
summary: Universal cross-splat artifact: an immense black pearl created by the Primordial Autochthon that suppresses all physical and magical turbulence for miles around and grants its wielder god-like, Storyteller-adjudicated reality-editing power over Manses, Demesnes, and the stable lands of Creation.
requirements: None stated beyond possession; using it to perform any specific effect requires an Essence + Occult roll (see mechanics).
mechanics: The Eye of Autochthon surpasses all other magic items known, having been itself created by the Primordial Autochthon. Through the Eye, mortals can tap a tiny fraction of a power older than the world or gods or time itself -- if they dare. The Eye looks like an immense black pearl, so large that a hero might strain to wrap his arms around it. Its ebon luster draws the eye into limitless depths of dark surface, a void that could birth worlds. No force, whether natural or divine, could so much as scratch the Eye's surface, but in the First Age some unknown agency clamped the great globe into a tight-fitting nest of gimbaled rings so that the Eye could turn freely in all directions, with no need to hand-push it; nevertheless it spins by itself. System: The Eye's active powers can be summarized as a 'plot device': it can do whatever the Storyteller wants it to; in general, its history shows it can create, destroy, or usurp control of Manses and Demesnes, and can transform the stable lands of the Realm and Threshold, though it cannot transform the looser, more Essence-soaked reality of the Wyld or the shadowlands. Its passive power to suppress all disturbances of land, sea, air, and magical turbulence for a league around it operates automatically and needs no roll: no wind blows above a mild, steady breeze, no one in the area suffers Wyld contamination, charms and sorcery have normal immediate effects but any continuing effect has its duration cut in half as the Eye reorders local Essence, and magical storms, waves, and earthquakes fail or stabilize. The Eye demands great expenditure of Essence: usurping control of a Manse, for instance, might require the player to expend 15 motes for every dot of the Manse's power (how an un-Exalted prophet once used it remains a mystery). The Eye also demands great skill to use: the player must succeed at an Essence + Occult roll at +2 difficulty to discover a new use for the Eye, and roll a simple success to perform that same feat thereafter. Any botch means the character suffers some bizarre and very permanent doom -- possibly affecting everyone within a mile or so, depending on the Storyteller's mood. The Eye does not function as an instant enemy-killer: the Primordial's power does not operate on so focused a scale, and any target smaller than a castle is too puny for the Eye to affect directly.
cost: Variable (e.g. 15 motes per dot of a Manse's power to usurp it); Essence + Occult roll at +2 difficulty to learn a new use, simple success thereafter
compatibility: Any possessor, Exalted or not (an un-Exalted prophet, Ikerre, once wielded it), of any splat including Abyssals; a Storyteller-adjudicated 'plot device' artifact rather than a routinely player-purchasable Background item -- best used as a rare, campaign-defining relic rather than a starting-character purchase.
notes: DERIVED FROM LUNAR'S VERIFIED TRANSCRIPTION (artifact-eye-of-autochthon): re-cited to Exalted Storyteller's Companion directly, no independent re-read. Chapter Four: Further Wonders, 'Eye of Autochthon (Artifact N/A)', printed p. 80 (PDF 81), the last entry in the chapter and the last mechanical content in the book, is a universal cross-splat artifact catalog entry with no splat-restricting language. Rated 'N/A' in the source rather than a numeric Artifact dot rating, reflecting its explicit framing as a Storyteller plot device; recorded here as 'selectable' per Lunar's own row's judgment call (a genuine named artifact a character could conceivably acquire, even if GM-adjudicated in play) rather than 'gm-only', preserving that same reasoning for Abyssal.

name: Cargo Preservation Spindles (Artifact • to •••, depending on size)
summary: A set of four five-sided jade-and-metal spindles, set into the corners of a hold or room, that protects cargo and food stores inside from rot, vermin, water damage, and theft for as long as it remains within the warded area.
requirements: None beyond ownership and the introduction ritual described in mechanics; usable by anyone, Exalted or not.
mechanics: Cargo preservation spindles come in a set of four, ranging in size from slender spires a handbreadth high to slender pillars nearly as tall as a man; despite the size range they share the same basic form, a five-sided spindle coming to a sharp point at either end, with the shorter end normally set into a socket carved into the decking or a specially placed holder. One is placed in each corner of the room or hold where cargo is kept; how large a spindle is determines how much area it protects, from a small passenger cabin up to a full cargo hold. To use the spindles, the owner must first introduce them to the cargo: the long end of each spindle is forced into the corresponding corner of the crate to be protected (far enough to leave a mark, not far enough to damage the crate or contents), and as this is done the contents are described in general detail -- radically different materials from those described will not be protected (a smuggler's hidden firedust can be totally ruined even while the rest of the cargo stays dry and intact). Once done, the cargo is protected from almost all manner of damage: food will neither rot, spoil, nor be infected or eaten by vermin (though food removed from its container ages and decays normally); water, even the thickest brine, cannot affect the goods; crates stay in place under all but the heaviest seas and, even if toppled, their contents remain undamaged. The spindles do not prevent theft, but anyone touching a warded crate or package will immediately know if anything has been taken from it. Protection holds as long as the cargo remains within the confines of the area bounded by the four spindles; a container removed from that area is no longer protected until it is returned (though nothing suddenly spoils the moment it leaves, e.g. previously-protected food does not instantly rot). Spindles are carefully faceted prisms of each of the five types of jade bound together with bands of orichalcum and pins of moonsilver, each facet carved with the symbol of the aligned Elemental Dragon plus requests for protection and a description of the warded contents.
compatibility: Any owner, Exalted or not, of any splat including Abyssals; still in general production today, though the difficulty of getting quantities of moonsilver or orichalcum limits new manufacture. Large numbers survive from the First Age, and many ships -- particularly those of the Realm -- carry one or more sets to protect belongings and cargo.
notes: Chapter Four: Creatures, Gods, Charms and Artifacts, 'Artifacts of the Waves' section header, 'Cargo Preservation Spindles (Artifact • to •••, depending on size)', printed p. 123 (PDF 124), Savage Seas. Transcribed directly from the rendered source PDF (image-based, no selectable text layer). This is the first entry in the Artifacts of the Waves catalog, immediately preceding Armor of Aquatic Puissance; a universal item with no splat-restricting text of any kind, so recorded as selectable for Abyssal without qualification.

name: Armor of Aquatic Puissance (Artifact ••••)
summary: A First Age suit of articulated plate inlaid with sparkling black jade whose locking helm lets the wearer breathe and see normally underwater and swim without penalty; the source text explicitly states no Abyssal is known to own a suit of this armor.
requirements: None to wear beyond ownership; the helm must be locked in place to gain the breathing/sight/swimming benefits.
mechanics: Soak: 10L/12B. Mobility Penalty: -2/0. Fatigue Value: 1. Commitment: 8. These curious suits of articulated plate armor are inlaid with a rare form of sparkling black jade that glistens even in the sun, built with tolerances and stresses that cannot be duplicated today -- all known suits date from before the Contagion. The helm is a massive casque, a single blue jewel that locks the shoulder yoke with a twist; the rest of the armor (excepting the faceplate) is worked in an ornate scale-and-fin pattern resembling the face of a fierce, bearded, angry warrior. Although not as strong as other enchanted articulated plate, it has advantages that make it extremely useful to Exalted who spend much time on the waves: when the helm is locked in place, the wearer breathes normally even in the deepest waters (limited only by Stamina + Endurance hours before it must be removed, since the armor does not deal with other needs such as food and water); the wearer can alter the armor's buoyancy at will to surface or sink; the armor doubles the wearer's normal swimming rate underwater with no mobility penalty (though ranged combat underwater remains as difficult as it would be for someone not wearing it); and the wearer sees underwater as clearly as in open air (clouds of silt, squid ink, and similar materials still block vision, just as fog or smoke would above water). The armor has sockets for two Hearthstones.
compatibility: Not as common as some conventional armor types, but does exist in some numbers: the Imperial Navy and the forces of Lookshy are known to have several suits, the more aquatically inclined Dynastic houses each have at least a couple, a number are rumored to be in the hands of the Guild, and the Lintha pirates are known to have at least two; Outcaste pirates or merchants may quietly own others. THE SOURCE TEXT STATES VERBATIM: 'No Abyssal is known to own a suit of this armor (unsurprisingly), but the deathknights each have comparable suits of their own design and manufacture.'
notes: Chapter Four: Creatures, Gods, Charms and Artifacts, 'Artifacts of the Waves', 'Armor of Aquatic Puissance (Artifact ••••)', printed p. 124 (PDF 125), Savage Seas. Transcribed directly from the rendered source PDF (image-based, no selectable text layer). MARKED reference-only RATHER THAN selectable, PER EXPLICIT PROJECT-OWNER INSTRUCTION: the book's own text states 'No Abyssal is known to own a suit of this armor (unsurprisingly)' -- unlike every other artifact in this section, this one is affirmatively flagged in-setting as something deathknights do not possess (the text immediately clarifies deathknights instead field their own comparable armor of independent design/manufacture, presumably already covered by this splat's own Backgrounds/Artifact catalog rather than this specific named item). Recorded here for completeness (a real, fully-statted named artifact from the book's universal-catalog chapter) but not offered as a selectable acquisition on an Abyssal character sheet, since taking it would contradict the source's own explicit setting fact. Still cited/tracked so a future GM wanting an in-fiction exception (e.g. a deathknight who looted a suit from a slain Terrestrial) has the full stat block on hand.

name: Steelsilk Sails (Artifact ••)
summary: Rare, near-indestructible sails supposedly woven from the silk of wood spiders or spider spirits, prized for the speed and agility they grant a ship in the wind and their near-total resistance to storms, fire, and mundane weapons.
requirements: A ship with sails to replace; the art of manufacturing steelsilk sails has been lost, so only pre-existing sets can be acquired.
mechanics: Highly sought after by those who favor speed and agility in the wind and water in battle, these rare sails are supposedly made out of the silk of wood spiders or spider spirits. Gossamer fine and light but strong as metal, steelsilk is nonetheless very stiff and makes poor armor. The art of manufacturing steelsilk sails has been lost, though those who possess them guard them jealously, often keeping them locked up except when the ship needs speed above all else. Steelsilk sails are most renowned for their ability to withstand punishment: storms that would leave silk sails in tatters, fires that would turn wet canvas sails to ash, and weapons that would cut ordinary reinforced canvas into ribbons all fail to damage steelsilk.
